record.name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design
record.approach: Spherical diffusion flames on a porous spherical burner, in drop towers and on the ISS, in two rounds. Normal flames (April to July 2019): ethylene, pure or diluted with nitrogen, flows from the burner into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. Inverse flames (November 2021 to February 2022): an oxygen/nitrogen mixture of up to 85 % oxygen flows from the burner into a chamber filled with nitrogen and ethylene. One extra normal-flame day with propane (28 October 2021) was used to calibrate optical temperature measurements. Reactant flow rate was held constant in each test, or ramped in selected tests.
record.conditions_note: The O2 range combines two configurations; see test_summary. In normal flames O2 is the chamber atmosphere (about 20 to 40 %), at about 0.93 to 1.3 atm. In inverse flames O2 is the gas leaving the burner (21 to 85 %) while the chamber holds ethylene and nitrogen with no oxygen, so 85 % is not an ambient oxygen level; pressures there range from about 0.43 to 3 atm. The chamber pressure limit was raised from 1.5 to 3 atm in January 2022 for the last inverse-flame days.
record.flow: no forced external flow; gas issues radially from the burner at a constant flow rate (total 0.3 to about 21.5 mg/s in normal flames; about 1.8 to 13.8 mg/s in inverse flames), or ramped in selected tests
record.geometry: porous stainless-steel spherical burner, 6.35 mm diameter, in the ACME chamber insert; spherical flame around the burner
record.gravity_note: ISS, plus earlier drop tower tests; the flames need far longer than drop towers allow (burn times up to 870 s were observed)
record.hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), after the rack was reconfigured for ACME. Porous spherical burner, retracting igniter, short (far) thermocouple rake on all days except the propane day, which used the long (near) rake. Burner heating limits test duration: tests end when the porous sphere reaches its temperature limit.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigators: Peter B. Sunderland (University of Maryland, Fire Protection Engineering), David Urban (NASA GRC). Investigator: Sergey Frolov (Semenov Institute of Chemical Physics, Russian Academy of Sciences; joint experiment Flame Design - Adamant). Phillip H. Irace (then a doctoral student) led much of the ISS data analysis.
record.objective: For spherical diffusion flames of gaseous fuel in microgravity: (A) find the limits at which soot starts to form, as a function of flow rate, mixture, amount of inert gas and pressure; (B) measure flame temperature, size, color and soot, and test whether steady flames can exist; (C) find extinction limits and the temperatures at which they occur, and tell radiative extinction from kinetic extinction.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: the normal-flame tests cover ambient oxygen of about 20, 30 and 40 % near 1 atm, so they bracket the oxygen level expected for the lunar base (about 30 % or more), though not its reduced pressure. The inverse-flame tests cover pressures from about 0.43 to 3 atm, but with oxygen supplied from the burner. The fuel is gas on a burner, not a solid material, so it informs models rather than material selection.
record.space_benefits: Radiative extinction is of fundamental importance in microgravity, where there is no buoyant flow. The critical extinction temperature and mass flux give simple criteria for predicting whether a flame will sustain itself or go out, which supports predictive modeling of fire scenarios.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with drop tower tests and a transient numerical model
record.earth_benefits: Potential to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant (soot) emissions in combustors on Earth; the work is contributing to designs of future coal power plants.
record.funding: NASA: NCC-3697, NCC-1063, NNC06AA32A, NNX09AO53A, NNX15AC75A, 80NSSC20M0072
record.hypothesis: (1) Soot forms only where the local carbon-to-oxygen ratio and temperature exceed critical values and the strain rate is low enough. (2) Microgravity spherical diffusion flames extinguish when the peak temperature first falls below 1130 K. (3) Steady-state spherical diffusion flames are possible.
record.principal_investigator: Richard L. Axelbaum (Washington University in St. Louis)
data_quality_notes: Rows marked RAMP, RAMPED or LOW O2 have no fixed flow or composition values in the table.
The 20 propane tests (day 13) list nominal values only (40 % oxygen, no final composition or pressure).
One inverse test ID reads 22042 where the neighbouring rows read 22024; probably a typo.

The final report is dated April 2023 and states that data analysis was still under way. The 1130 K result is reported for tests at about 1 bar; a 2024 publication in the list covers elevated pressure.
key_results: All the ISS flames extinguished at the same critical temperature of 1130 K, across a broad range of oxygen levels, dilution and flow rates at about 1 bar.

Extinction also occurs at a fixed reactant mass flux: 0.2 g/m2-s of fuel for normal flames and 0.68 g/m2-s of oxygen for inverse flames. From these, a simple equation estimates the flame size at extinction from the reactant flow rate alone.

In microgravity a flame at constant flow keeps growing; as it grows it radiates more, cools, and goes out when radiative heat loss approaches the heat released (radiative extinction). The report notes this has implications for spacecraft fire safety.
Before going out, a flame may oscillate: part of it extinguishes and reforms, with growing amplitude, until complete extinction.

Steady-state spherical flames can exist in microgravity despite radiative loss, if the steady flame size is smaller than the size for radiative extinction. Flames showing steady behavior were observed for up to 870 s.
Sufficiently small flames with low radiative losses burn quasi-steadily; test duration is then limited by burner heating, not by the flame going out.

The chamber pressure limit was raised to 3 atm for the last test days because pressure was found to be a critical variable for predicting extinction; the principal investigator noted that extinction data over a wide pressure range could be valuable for spacecraft fire safety.

record.name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Burning Rate Emulator
record.approach: A flat burner fed with gaseous fuel (ethylene, pure or diluted with nitrogen, and methane) emulates a burning solid or liquid surface. Heat flux back to the burner is measured; heat flux divided by fuel flow gives the effective heat of gasification. Flow rate, ambient oxygen and pressure were varied. Round 1 (February to April 2019) used only the 25 mm burner and ethylene; Round 2 (September 2020 to January 2021) added the 50 mm burner and methane (not together). Most long tests were ended by cutting the fuel after about 3 minutes (one flame ran 5 minutes); others self-extinguished. Results were combined with an analytical flame model, a radiation correlation and the RADCAL model to build flammability maps.
record.conditions_note: Nominal oxygen levels were 21, 25 (Round 2), 26.5, 34 and 40 %; measured values per test ranged from about 18 to 39 %. Pressures were nominally 14.7, 10.2 and 8.2 psia (1, 0.7 and 0.565 bar). Two conditions match NASA candidate exploration atmospheres: 26.5 % O2 at 10.2 psia and 34 % O2 at 8.2 psia. The 40 % O2 tests were at 14.7 psia. Constant-volume chamber of about 85 L free volume, so oxygen is consumed during long burns.
record.flow: no forced external flow (quiescent chamber); fuel issues from the burner face at a constant mass flux of about 1 to 12 g/m2-s
record.geometry: flat round burners of 25 mm and 50 mm diameter; copper face with 125 holes of 1.2 mm acting as a calorimeter, ceramic flow straightener, 1 mm stainless-steel sidewalls; dome-shaped flame above the burner
record.gravity_note: ISS. Drop towers (5.2 s) are too short: the gas phase needs about 20 s and the burner surface about 40 s to approach steady state.
record.hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack: nominally 100 L chamber, about 15 L filled by hardware. Resistively heated, retractable igniter. Nitrogen-calibrated Hastings mass flow controllers (Wright 2021: HFM-300, 0.2 or 0.5 slpm full scale; Dehghani 2022 names model HFC-302D). Two embedded Medtherm heat flux gauges, copper calorimeter face, Dexter Research 2M wide-angle radiometers (BRE array, later replaced by the ACME array), photomultiplier tubes, thin-filament pyrometry, operations camera and ACME camera. Data per test day limited to about 127,000 MB downlink.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigators: Peter B. Sunderland (University of Maryland) and John L. de Ris (FM Global, retired). Parham Dehghani (doctoral student, University of Maryland) did much of the ISS analysis; Anna E. Wright (MS 2021) analysed extinction times. Fumiaki Takahashi (CWRU) was Deputy Project Scientist in preparatory drop testing; Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam (CWRU) were on the NASA science team for flight operations. Lead Russian collaborator: Alexander Y. Snegirev.
record.objective: Establish the burning conditions of condensed fuels in a quiescent microgravity atmosphere in terms of material properties: (1) observe long-duration burning of CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 on porous burners of 25 and 50 mm in O2/N2 atmospheres, including NASA's candidate crew atmospheres (14.7 psia / 21 %, 10.2 psia / 26.5 %, 8.2 psia / 34 % O2); (2) repeat in O2/CO2 atmospheres (desired; not done, NASA did not include it); (3) find extinction limits. Gas flames emulate solids and liquids by matching their heats of combustion and gasification.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: tests cover 21 to 40 % oxygen at 0.565 to 1 bar, including 26.5 % at 10.2 psia and 34 % at 8.2 psia, so they bracket both the oxygen level and the reduced pressure expected for a lunar base. The fuel is gas on a burner emulating solids, so conclusions about specific materials rest on modeling.
record.space_benefits: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to materials such as PMMA and nylon was found without any air flow, while stopping ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. This was seen in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft. The authors suggest NASA may want to use its cone calorimeter flammability test (NASA-STD-6001B Test 2) more, because it measures the properties that set microgravity burning.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with normal-gravity and drop tower tests and analytical/radiation modeling
record.funding: NASA ISS Research Program, agreement 80NSSC20M0119 (cited in Wright 2021); other awards not listed in the sources read
record.principal_investigator: James G. Quintiere (University of Maryland, Fire Protection Engineering)
fuel: ethylene (C2H4), pure or diluted with nitrogen; heats of combustion 15 to 47.2 kJ/g in the dissertation data, 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g in Round 1
methane (CH4), pure or diluted with nitrogen (Round 2, 25 mm burner only)
data_quality_notes: Flame counts are inconsistent: the final report's Table 1 sums to 194 (62 + 132) while its text and Wright 2021 say 196; the dissertation uses 59, 103, 146 and 149 for different subsets, and both 46 and 49 for fuel-terminated flames.
Round 2 start differs between sources: September 2020 (final report), August 2020 (Wright 2021), July 2020 (Stocker 2021).
The dissertation's Round 1 chapter says pressures of '1 to about 0.4 bar', but its test design table and the final report give 0.56 to 1 bar.

The '3 to 4 times lower than normal gravity' burning rate is an average: at 25 mm, normal-gravity data give PMMA about 19 g/m2-s and PE/PP about 6 g/m2-s, against about 2.5 and 3 g/m2-s predicted for microgravity.
Radiometers often saturated (most BRE-array sensors in Round 1, many in Round 2), so radiative loss data come mainly from smaller flames and the +60 mm/offset sensors.

Water vapor condensed on the uncooled heat flux sensors below the 60 to 70 C dew point and then re-evaporated; for short methane burns this did not clear, so heat of gasification could not be computed.
Heating through the exposed edge of the copper calorimeter inflated raw heat flux by up to 3 times before correction.
The two radiative loss fits are nearly the same curve over the data range, not independent evidence.
The 1100 to 1200 K extinction temperature comes from four flames.
Uncertainty analysis (dissertation): heat of gasification 4.5 to 17.5 % (mean 5.7 %), fuel mass flux 1.3 to 17 % (mean 3.1 %).
A third-party repository lists the DOI as 10.60555/vb93-3y72 (not verified).
key_results: All flames in 21 % oxygen self-extinguished within 40 s, and flames at nominal 25 % within 90 s. Quasi-steady flames were observed at nominal oxygen of 26.5 % and above (26.5, 34 and 40 %), including two NASA candidate exploration atmospheres.

Steady burning at elevated oxygen was not universal: small flames could burn for minutes, larger ones generally self-extinguished within about 1.5 minutes. Methane flames were harder to ignite and self-extinguished within a minute in all conditions, so burn time depends on fuel chemistry.

The 49 fuel-terminated flames reached on average 0.953 of their computed steady height (standard deviation 0.019) and more than 94 % of steady heat flux; self-extinguished flames reached only about 0.5 to 0.9.
Two extinction limits were found on a heat of combustion against heat of gasification map: radiative extinction for large flames and quenching for small flames.

Thin-filament pyrometry on four flames, confirmed by simulations, gave a critical extinction temperature of 1100 to 1200 K. The literature value for buoyant normal-gravity flames is about 1600 K, which corresponds to a strain rate near 10 1/s, against about 1 1/s for 1100 K.

Radiative loss fraction reached about 60 % in microgravity against about 30 % in normal gravity, and was correlated with a dimensionless radiation parameter Omega (Xr = 0.49 Omega^0.12, R^2 = 0.87; or Xr = 0.0633 ln(Omega) + 0.452).
Ethylene flames, which soot in normal gravity, did not soot in microgravity except briefly at ignition; nitrogen dilution reduced soot.
Pressure had only a weak effect on the quality of burning, but changes radiative loss through the partial pressures of H2O and CO2.
Extinction time correlated with t = A * X_O2^3.42 * Re^-0.424 (R^2 = 0.61), independent of pressure: higher oxygen and lower fuel flow gave longer-lasting flames (Wright 2021).

From flammability maps the authors infer that polyethylene and polypropylene would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2-s, nylon and PMMA at about 2.5 g/m2-s and phenolic glass fiber at about 1 g/m2-s; materials with heats of combustion of 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification of about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn. This is an inference from emulation and theory, not a test of those materials.

record.name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
record.approach: Methane and ethylene diffusion flames, often diluted with nitrogen, issue from a central nozzle into a surrounding air coflow, over a wide range of conditions; fuel and air velocities are typically matched, and lifted flames are studied so the flame does not depend on heat loss to the burner. Planned diagnostics (PSI record, written in the future tense): OH* and CH* chemiluminescence to follow lift-off height and flame shape as extinction is approached; soot luminosity and laser extinction for soot temperature and volume fraction in fuel-rich flames; thin-filament pyrometry for gas temperature in non-sooting regions. Model kinetics and soot sub-models are then adjusted to match. ISS operations ran in three periods: November 2017 to February 2018, May to September 2018, and February to March 2021 (NASA ACME overview).
record.conditions_note: The oxidizer is an air coflow; oxygen level and chamber pressure per test are not documented in the parts of the record that were read. Constant-volume chamber.
record.flow: forced coaxial flow: fuel from the nozzle and an air coflow around it, velocities typically matched; values not in this summary. The log lists only the full-scale rating of the installed mass flow controller (0.1 slpm on a nitrogen basis), not the flow used.
record.geometry: coflow burner in the ACME chamber insert: central fuel nozzle surrounded by an air coflow; dimensions not in this summary
record.gravity_note: ISS
record.hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack: nominally 100 L chamber, about 83 L free. Crew-exchangeable mass flow controllers. Available diagnostics include a calibrated high-definition color camera (CH* concentration, flame and soot temperature by pyrometry, soot volume fraction), a gray-scale camera with an opposed collimated light source (light-extinction soot volume fraction), intensified cameras for OH* and CH*, photomultiplier tubes, a thermopile radiometer array and a translating array of 14-micrometer silicon carbide fibers for thin-filament pyrometry. Which of these were used on each CLD test day is not stated here.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigator: Mitchell D. Smooke (Yale University). Proposal title: 'Fuel Dilution Studies of Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flames in a Microgravity Environment'. Lead Russian collaborator (from NASA's ACME overview, not the PSI record): Sergey S. Minaev. The precursor experiment was SLICE (Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment), run in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox in January to March 2012.
record.objective: Provide experimental data for rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum: (A) characterize weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through flame shape, lift-off height, temperature and extinction limits; (B) characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through flame shape, gas temperature in the soot-free part of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperature and soot volume fraction.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: oxygen and pressure per test are not documented here, and the study is primarily fundamental (model validation), so its link to a lunar base scenario is indirect.
record.space_benefits: Indirect: validated soot and extinction sub-models feed the fire models used in spacecraft safety analysis. Soot production is much stronger in microgravity, which affects flame radiation and smoke.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), to provide benchmark data for computational models of chemical kinetics and soot
record.earth_benefits: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices; predicting the coupling of transport and detailed chemistry is critical for modeling turbulent reacting flows, soot formation and radiation. Understanding diffusion flame extinction matters for fire suppression and engine efficiency. Microgravity removes buoyancy, which complicates both experiments and models in normal gravity.
record.hypothesis: Not stated as a testable hypothesis: the PSI record says the investigation gathered benchmark data to validate computational models, described in earlier publications by Smooke, Long and co-workers (Combust. Theory Model. 2004; Combust. Flame 2000; Proc. Combust. Inst. 2000 and 1998).
fuel: methane (CH4), diluted with nitrogen (25 to 40 % in the visible log rows)
data_quality_notes: No final report exists; the PSI record (description and experimental table) is the primary source.

The experimental table labels fuel bottles '40% CH4', '40% CH5', '40% CH6', '40% CH7' and '40% CH8' on consecutive rows. These species do not exist; they are almost certainly spreadsheet auto-increment errors for 40% CH4 (all rows are 'Methane based test'). Inferred, not confirmed by NASA.
The fuel bottle is 40 % CH4 in N2, further diluted on orbit to 25 to 40 % fuel; concentration was varied between and sometimes during tests.
The MFC columns give the full-scale rating of the installed fuel and nitrogen controllers (0.1 slpm, nitrogen basis), not the flows used.
Only the first 5 of 33 rows were visible in the saved page, all methane; the notes column is cut off after 'However'. The full table is in PSI-21_Experimental table_CLD Flame.csv.
Most publications on the record predate the ISS flights (ground studies and the 2012 SLICE precursor); the 2022 Dobbins et al. paper is the one listed by NASA as including ISS results.
The record lists one publication twice (Cao et al., doi 10.1016/j.proci.2014.05.138).

record.name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
record.approach: A voltage of up to 10 kV, of either sign, was applied between the burner and a copper mesh above it. In each test a flame was ignited, allowed to settle, and the voltage was swept in small steps or ramps while ion current, light emission and images were recorded. Round 1 (March to May 2018) used the coflow burner with and without a weak air flow; round 2 (September to November 2018) used a simple gas-jet burner. Fuels were methane and ethylene, pure or diluted with nitrogen. Tests were commanded from the ground with scripts.
record.conditions_note: Chamber atmosphere and coflow were synthetic air (21 % O2, 79 % N2 by volume) in all tests, at a nominal 100 kPa (14.5 psi). Pressure was measured but per-test values are not in the PSI table. Tests are constant-volume, so pressure rises slightly and oxygen falls during a test. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is a nominal value (cabin room temperature, about 25 °C), assumed by the team; it was not measured or reported for these tests.
record.flow: Coflow burner tests with a weak coflow of synthetic air (21/79 O2/N2 by volume), e.g. 3.1 cm/s, or with no coflow (0 cm/s); gas-jet burner tests with the fuel jet issuing into the quiescent chamber atmosphere (same synthetic air). Fuel jet velocities of e.g. 15, 19 and 27 cm/s. The applied field drives an ion wind upward (mesh negative, positive ions toward the mesh) or toward the burner (mesh positive), which can push the flame down onto the burner.
record.geometry: Laminar non-premixed jet flames on the axis of the 0.4 m diameter ACME chamber insert, with a flat circular copper mesh electrode downstream of the burner. (1) Coflow burner (same as CLD Flame): stainless fuel tube ID 2.16 mm (nominal 2.2 mm), OD 2.41 mm, protruding 3.1 mm beyond the annulus outlet; outer tube ID 25 mm; annulus outlet is a 6.4 mm thick Hastelloy X honeycomb (0.81 mm cells, 0.05 mm foil). Mesh 37 mm above the fuel tube outlet (alternate position 52 mm, not used). (2) Gas-jet burner ('2.1 mm'): same tubing, ID 2.16 mm, OD 2.41 mm, mesh nominally 35 mm downstream. Mesh: 8.9 cm diameter with copper ring (8.4 cm without), square copper weave of 7.1 wires/cm, 0.43 mm wire diameter, 48% open area. Retractable resistively heated hot-wire igniter with crew-exchangeable tip and stepper-motor radial drive.
record.gravity_note: ISS, with comparison tests in normal gravity
record.hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack (chamber about 100 L, about 90 L free), with the coflow or gas-jet burner, retracting igniter, high-voltage power supplies (one polarity installed at a time) and a removable copper mesh electrode 35 to 37 mm above the burner.
record.investigators_note: University project scientist: Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien (UC Irvine). Co-Investigators: Felix Weinberg (Imperial College London, died 2012) and Sunny Karnani. Lead collaborator: Sergey Minaev (Far Eastern Federal University). NASA science team: Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam (CWRU); Fumiaki Takahashi was deputy project scientist for drop testing.
record.objective: Gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how an electric field (ion-driven wind) can be used to control non-premixed flames. Specific objectives: (A) determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane, ethylene) flow rate and nitrogen dilution; (B) obtain the time response of flame chemiluminescence, luminosity and ion current to large step changes in voltage; (C) evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to field voltage and ion current; (D) use the ion current vs. voltage behavior to characterize near-limit lifted flames and use the ion-driven wind to stabilize or reattach them.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: All tests in 21 % O2 near 1 atm, with gas fuels on a burner. It adds understanding of flame control by electric fields, not flammability limits.
record.space_benefits: Not aimed at a space application, but the findings could help future space combustion devices, for example for solid waste processing.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with normal-gravity laboratory tests
record.earth_benefits: Electric fields could allow stable, leaner burner operation with less soot and pollutant emission, and more efficient combustion.
record.hypothesis: Electric fields applied in microgravity will strongly influence laminar diffusion flames, allowing flame stability, soot behavior and combustion to be controlled through the ion-driven wind and chemi-ionization.
data_quality_notes: O2: the chamber atmosphere and the coflow were synthetic air, 21% O2 / 79% N2 by volume, in all tests (no O2 variation). Some vitiation occurs during each constant-volume test.

Pressure: nominal 100 kPa (14.5 psi) in the final report; pressure was measured (chamber pressure sensor) but per-test values are not in the experimental table. The CIR chamber can operate up to 300 kPa.

Hardware changes before flight: the 1.3 mm jet burner was dropped (fall 2016); coflow-burner tests were added to compensate for the slow HVPS; polarity switching within a test was dropped because of electromagnetic interference.
Thin Filament Pyrometry (14 µm SiC fibers) was not used because the fibers interfere with the electric field.

Anomalies: IPSU-G drive failure (2018-04-27, recovered 2018-05-07); IPSU-1/HiBMs unavailable on 2018-09-26 and 2018-10-01; heavy soot deposited on the coflow burner after the last positive-mesh ethylene day (2018-05-17), cleaned by the crew on 2018-06-19; MFC flow oscillations.
The last test day (2018-11-15, 100% C2H4 bottle diluted to 25/50/80/100%) appears twice in the PSI experimental table; it is counted once (11 flames).
ambient_temperature_K = 298 is nominal (assumed), not a measurement.
key_results: In microgravity the V-I curve shows a distinct ion-current peak at the most compact flame, then a drop to a lower saturation plateau; 1-g flames rise smoothly to saturation.
Peak ion current is roughly proportional to fuel flow velocity and increases with coflow; it is higher in microgravity than in comparable 1-g flames.
The electric body force can produce flame oscillations similar to buoyant flicker, and microgravity flames under a field can mimic 1-g flame shapes.
With the gas-jet burner and an upward ion wind the V-I curve is parabolic, unlike the coflow burner; reversing polarity does not give an inverted result.
Soot plus electric field gives complex behavior: soot elimination, showers of incandescent particles, unstable 'dancing' flames, and soot deposits on the burner and mesh.

record.name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames
record.approach: Fuel mixed with a diluent flowed out of a porous spherical burner into a still oxidizing atmosphere and was ignited to give a roughly spherical flame. The flow rate was held or ramped up or down to drive the flame to extinction. Round 1 (September 2019 to January 2020) used nitrogen as the diluent for both fuel and atmosphere; round 2 (May to July 2020) used helium. Tests were commanded from the ground with scripts and ended when the flame went out or the burner reached 250 C.
record.conditions_note: Nominal values from the PSI table: about 21 % or about 30 % O2 in nitrogen or helium at about 1 atm. Tests are constant-volume, so pressure rises and oxygen falls slightly as the day's tests consume it. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is a nominal value (cabin room temperature, about 25 °C), assumed by the team; it was not measured or reported for these tests.
record.flow: Quiescent ambient (no forced convection); flame driven only by the burner outflow. Burner flow rates from ~1 to ~17.5 cc/s, held steady or ramped up/down during a test to reach radiative (high flow) or kinetic (low flow) extinction. Fuel MFC up to 2 slpm (N2 basis; a 0.5 slpm fuel MFC limited some methane tests); oxidizer up to 20 slpm and nitrogen up to 5 slpm for chamber filling.
record.geometry: Nominally spherical, one-dimensional diffusion flame around a porous spherical burner of 6.35 mm diameter (sintered porous sphere on a supply tube) on the axis of the ACME chamber insert (~0.4 m diameter) in the CIR chamber (free volume ~83–90 L); fuel/diluent issues outward into a quiescent oxidizing atmosphere. At high flow rates the flow was not spherically symmetric (more flow through the sphere–tube joint), giving offset, ellipsoidal or parabolic flames. Ignition by a retractable resistive igniter (loop tip in round 1, coil tip in round 2 except its first day).
record.gravity_note: ISS, plus earlier drop tower tests that were too short to show extinction
record.hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack (free volume about 83 to 90 L), with the 6.35 mm porous spherical burner, retracting igniter (loop tip, then coil tip for helium), fiber array for pyrometry and the short (far) thermocouple rake. Tests end when the burner reaches its 250 C limit.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigators: Stephen D. Tse (Rutgers University) and Kurt R. Sacksteder (NASA GRC). Lead collaborator: Vladimir V. Gubernov (P.N. Lebedev Physical Institute). NASA science team: Vedha Nayagam and Uday G. Hegde (CWRU); Fumiaki Takahashi was deputy project scientist for drop testing.
record.objective: In soot-free and sooty flames, and in comparison with detailed computational simulation (transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics, including chemiluminescence): (A) measure and characterize the transient structure (temperature, species distribution) of spherical diffusion flames that start from a non-steady state, for H2/CH4/diluent mixtures (soot-free) and C2H4/diluent mixtures (sooty) at different flow rates; (B) determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler number) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler number); (C) determine the existence, onset and nature (mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities predicted for fuel/diluent mixtures above a critical Lewis number.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: Oxygen of about 21 and 30 % near 1 atm, with nitrogen or helium as diluent, so it includes the oxygen level and a helium atmosphere but not reduced pressure. The fuel is gas on a burner, so it informs models rather than material selection.
record.space_benefits: Shows that radiative extinction is common for flames in microgravity and gives extinction data for testing flame models.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with drop tower tests and transient numerical simulations
record.earth_benefits: Benchmark data for chemical kinetic and transport models of hydrogen, methane and ethylene flames.
record.hypothesis: A transient numerical simulation with detailed chemistry, transport and radiation can describe spherical diffusion flames. Each measured feature (flame growth, steady states, extinction, instabilities, soot limits) is a test of that model and of how complete its chemical kinetic and transport descriptions are.
data_quality_notes: O2 and pressure: the experimental table gives ~21% or ~30% O2 at ~1 atm, noting that pressure rises and O2 drops with vitiation; pressure_min_psi = pressure_max_psi = 14.7 is nominal.
The experimental table writes the diluent as 'N3', 'N4', 'N5', 'N6' on several rows; these are typos for N2.
Tests ended automatically when the burner reached its 250 °C temperature limit; the PSI flame counts neglect flames that quenched right after ignition.

Anomalies: leaking first fuel bottle quick-connect (2019-07-30); IPSU-G image storage problems causing lost image data in round 1; on 2020-05-11 (first He day) only 7 of 15 tests ignited because helium's high thermal conductivity needed much more igniter power, so the loop igniter tip was replaced by a sturdier coil tip.
The fuel MFC (0.5 slpm) was too small for quasi-steady 45% CH4 flames in air, so methane tests moved to 30% O2.
ambient_temperature_K = 298 is nominal (assumed), not a measurement.
key_results: N2-diluted CH4 and C2H4 flames in air showed both kinetic extinction at low flow rates and radiative extinction at high flow rates; radiative extinction was common on ISS, as predicted computationally but never seen in ground tests.
Example: 20% C2H4 / 80% N2 at 3 cc/s gave a quasi-steady flame; 5–10 cc/s gave radiative extinction; ramping down from 3 cc/s gave kinetic extinction before 1 cc/s.
Ethylene flames, sooty in 1 g, did not soot in microgravity except briefly during ignition, in any O2 level or diluent.
N2-diluted H2 flames would need very large sizes to self-extinguish; no radiative extinction was seen, but kinetic extinction on ramp-down was.
He dilution shifted the extinction limits, made ignition much harder and affected heat transfer to the burner; predicted pulsating instabilities were not conclusively observed in the video.
Flame luminosity does not necessarily reflect flame strength.

record.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
record.approach: Combustion tests on the ISS with real-time crew operation. Fuel samples were mounted in a small wind tunnel installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox, with airflow up to 40 cm/s. Oxygen was lowered below 21 % by adding nitrogen. Flame appearance, growth and spread rate were measured in both opposed and concurrent flow.
record.conditions_note: O2 range (13.6-22.2 %) is stated in the Summary Report and matches the 129 rows of the PSI experiment table. O2 was lowered by diluting the MSG working volume with nitrogen, a first on the ISS. Pressure: the report treats the working volume as 1 atm (ISS cabin); it was not varied. Ambient temperature is not stated.
record.flow: forced airflow from 0 to about 55 cm/s with no flow restrictor, about 35 cm/s with two restrictors; opposed, concurrent and stagnation-flow configurations; flow stepped up or down during a test to find quenching (low flow) and blowoff (high flow) limits
record.geometry: films and slabs 0.1 to 5 mm thick, 1 or 2 cm wide, one- and two-sided burning; rods 6.35, 9.525 and 12.7 mm diameter (1/4, 3/8, 1/2 inch), 57 mm long; section of a 4 cm diameter sphere; flat fabric samples 1 or 2 cm wide
record.gravity_note: ISS; results compared with normal-gravity tests in the publications
record.hardware_note: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in the Destiny lab, with the BASS-II flow duct: a 7.6 x 7.6 x 17 cm fan-driven duct originally built for gas-jet flame studies. Hot-wire igniter operated manually by the astronaut. MSG filters capture particulates and convert CO to CO2.
record.investigators_note: Roles taken from the BASS-II Summary Report (NASA/TM-20210011385). The PSI metadata lists the same people as Co-Investigators and omits Olson.
record.objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. Begin to bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity. Provide preliminary data to the SoFIE investigators. Examine practical, thicker fuels in typical geometries (slabs, cylinders, spherical sections). Results feed the computational models used to design fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: O2 range is 13.6-22.2 % at 1 atm, so it covers ISS-like atmospheres and the low-oxygen flammability limit, but not the roughly 30 % O2 at reduced pressure expected for the lunar base.
record.space_benefits: Improved spacecraft fire safety: helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future missions.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS)
record.earth_benefits: The simpler flame shape in microgravity lets researchers test computer models of burning fuel, which can then be applied to wildfires, building fires, energy recovery from waste and other combustion problems.
record.hypothesis: Materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well as or better than the same material in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions. NASA's upward-burning flammability test in normal gravity is treated as the worst case on Earth, but may not be conservative for space.

key_results: PMMA rods stay flammable in microgravity down to about 13.5 % O2, well below the 15.4 % upward flame spread limit measured in normal gravity. The standard ground flammability test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) is therefore not conservative for space.

The flammability boundary is U-shaped: flames quench at very low flow and blow off at high flow. The most flammable condition is at weak ventilation, which the report notes is typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces.
Opposed-flow flame spread over black PMMA rods occurred down to 17.5 % O2 in microgravity, against 19 % in normal gravity.
Ignition is harder than sustaining a flame: ignition limits lie at higher O2 than flammability limits, and ignition delay can be almost 10 times the igniter-on time of the NASA-STD-6001 test.
The three Nomex samples did not ignite. Nomex is widely used on the ISS as a fire barrier.
A burning wax candle ejected a droplet of molten wax upstream, illustrating how melting plastics can spread fire in microgravity.
For thin PMMA films, the critical opposed-flow velocity below which the flame goes out (radiative extinction) does not depend on fuel thickness, and it rises as O2 falls.
SIBAL fabric in concurrent flow quenched at flow velocities between 1 and 5 cm/s.
Thicker fuels spread flame more slowly; two-sided burning spreads faster than one-sided. The numerical model over-predicted spread rates for thick slabs.

Combustion products: O2 burned nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, but CO-to-CO2 ratios were about ten times those of efficient combustion and CO rose sharply near the low-O2 limit. Flames were fuel rich (global equivalence ratio about 1.3). First extensive data on the toxicity of combustion products in microgravity.
Most tests released well below 100 W of heat.

record.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids
record.approach: Solid samples were burned in a small flow duct (reused SPICE hardware) inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox. A hot wire ignited each sample; a fan set the air speed along the sample, with flow in the same direction as flame spread (concurrent), against it (opposed), or onto a sphere (stagnation or wake ignition). Air speed was changed during each burn to find extinction at low flow and blow-off at high flow, and a nitrogen jet was used to try to put flames out. In 2013 the glovebox was filled with nitrogen to lower the oxygen level. The Science Requirements Document (February 2010) planned four changes to the SPICE hardware: replaceable solid fuel samples, an adjustable igniter, a nitrogen gas jet for extinguishment and a way to shut the flow off completely. Each sample was to burn for about one minute, be photographed, and then be extinguished by stepping up the nitrogen flow.
record.conditions_note: Measured values from the ISS environment columns of the as-run test matrix. In 2012 the tests ran in ISS air (about 20.9 to 22.7 % O2). In 2013 the glovebox working volume was diluted with nitrogen to about 16 to 17.8 % O2. Pressure was not controlled (0.97 to 1.009 atm); CO2 was 1.37 to 3.51 mmHg. The SRD (2010) required the cabin O2 to be measured on each test day and restricted testing to 21 % O2 or more; the 2013 reduced-oxygen tests went beyond that original requirement. Pressure was specified only as ambient. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is a nominal value (cabin room temperature, about 25 °C), assumed by the team; it was not measured or reported for these tests.
record.flow: Forced air flow from a variable-speed fan along the fuel surface, from 0 (fan off) up to ~44 cm/s; concurrent, opposed and stagnation-point (spheres, with forward-stagnation or wake ignition) configurations; gaseous N2 (GN2) suppressant jet could be added into the flow. Requirements (SRD 2010): air speed adjustable from 5 to 50 cm/s, measured by an anemometer; nitrogen 0–500 sccm through a mass flow controller; the flow must be able to shut off completely as a safety measure to extinguish the flame.
record.geometry: Samples mounted in a small flow duct with a 7.6 cm x 7.6 cm square cross-section. SIBAL fabric: thin sheets 8.5 cm long, 1 or 2 cm wide, ~0.32 mm thick, area density ~18 mg/cm². PMMA spheres of 1 and 2 cm diameter. Flat PMMA slabs, Nomex and Ultem sheets (~2 cm wide), candles and flat wax slabs. Ignition by a 29-gauge Kanthal hot-wire igniter (pre-wired for fabrics; positioned at the stagnation region or in the wake for spheres).
record.gravity_note: ISS
record.hardware_note: Slightly modified SPICE flow duct (7.6 cm x 7.6 cm cross-section) in the Microgravity Science Glovebox, with a variable-speed fan, hot-wire igniters, a nitrogen suppressant line, a radiometer, a video camera and a digital still camera. SRD imaging requirements: color video from 20 mm upstream of the fuel to the end of the duct, and 2–3 high-resolution raw still images per test (at least 3000 x 2000 pixels).
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigators: Fumiaki Takahashi and James T'ien (Case Western Reserve University).
record.objective: 1) Bridge the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity, by observing flames over practical (thicker) fuels in typical geometries for the long times available in flight, including wake flames. 2) Assess the effectiveness of an inert gaseous extinguishing agent (nitrogen, similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating and flow conditions.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: Solid fuels in forced flow, with measured oxygen from about 16 to 22.7 % near 1 atm, plus nitrogen suppression. No tests above cabin oxygen and none at reduced pressure.
record.space_benefits: Spacecraft materials are selected with a normal-gravity test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1). BASS provides flammability and nitrogen-suppression data in real microgravity to check that method and to validate fire models for spacecraft design.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS)
record.earth_benefits: Validated combustion models apply to many combustion problems on Earth.
record.hypothesis: Materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well as or better than the same material in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions. Testing this for anything but the thinnest materials needs more microgravity time than drop towers or parabolic flights provide.
fuel: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric (75 % cotton, 25 % fiberglass by mass)

record.name: Cool Flames Investigation
record.approach: Same procedure and hardware as FLEX, with minor data acquisition changes. The crew installs the fuel syringe and gas bottles; everything else is run from the ground. The chamber is filled with the chosen gas at the chosen pressure, a droplet of about 4 mm is dispensed between two needles and freely deployed, then ignited by hot wires that retract once ignition is detected. When needed, a 40-micrometer silicon carbide fiber tethers the droplet to stop it drifting out of view. Large droplets first burn with a visible hot flame that goes out by radiative heat loss; burning can then continue as an invisible cool flame. Tests ran from January to September 2017.
record.conditions_note: Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3 and 5 atm; n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures from 0.5 to 5 atm; farnesane from 0.75 to 3 atm. Mostly in air (O2 mole fraction 0.21). Helium dilution of 29 % and 59 % with O2 at 0.21, helium replacing part of the nitrogen. A few tests at reduced oxygen (values not given in the report).
record.flow: no forced flow; quiescent chamber
record.geometry: spherically symmetric isolated droplet, initial diameter about 4 mm (e.g. 4.35 mm in FLEX-1268); free-floating, or tethered on a 40-micrometer silicon carbide fiber
record.gravity_note: ISS. Cool flames need much longer residence times than buoyant flames allow and cannot be observed with droplets in normal gravity.
record.hardware_note: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus in the Combustion Integrated Rack, same as FLEX with minor data acquisition modifications. Backlit black-and-white camera (5 x 5 cm field of view) for droplet size; UV-sensitive camera imaging OH* emission for flame size; color camera with live downlink; narrow-band and wide-band radiometers. Farouk et al. also describe an intensified camera with a rotating filter wheel (430 nm for CH* during the hot flame, 390 to 490 nm for formaldehyde during the cool flame) used on CFI tests such as FLEX-1268.
record.investigators_note: No principal investigator is named; the experiment was defined by a Science Definition Team: Forman A. Williams (UC San Diego), Frederick L. Dryer (Princeton), Tanvir I. Farouk (University of South Carolina), Vedha Nayagam (Case Western Reserve University) and Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA GRC). Russian collaborators: Sergey M. Frolov, Valentin Ya. Basevich, Sergey N. Medvedev, Andrey A. Belyaev. GRC project staff: Andrew Suttles (project manager), Daniel L. Dietrich (project scientist), Vedha Nayagam (staff scientist). Engineering by ZIN Technologies (Marty O'Toole, engineering manager). Final report by Nayagam and Dietrich, 23 July 2020.
record.objective: Further explore the quasi-steady cool flames discovered in FLEX: examine how fuel molecular structure, fuel mixtures and ambient conditions (pressure, helium dilution) affect cool-flame burning of n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures and farnesane. The stated final objective covered 0.25 to 5 atm; tests were run from 0.5 to 5 atm.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: oxygen was about 21 % in most tests, below the level expected for a lunar base, and re-ignition appears mainly above about 1.25 to 2 atm, above cabin pressure. The fuel is an isolated liquid hydrocarbon droplet, not a cabin material, so it informs models more than material selection.
record.space_benefits: A fire that looks extinguished may keep burning as an invisible cool or warm flame, which matters for fire detection and for deciding when a fire is out; unburned fuel vapor can also collect around the fuel in still air.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with detailed numerical modeling of droplet combustion
record.earth_benefits: Low-temperature chemistry controls autoignition and is central to engines such as HCCI that run cooler to cut pollution and raise efficiency; the CFI data help validate the chemical kinetic mechanisms being developed. Cool-flame combustion may also be useful in fuel reforming to produce hydrogen for fuel cells.
record.funding: Initiated by NASA through the Science Definition Team; peer reviewed and approved by NASA HQ as a follow-up to FLEX and FLEX-2. Related modeling supported by NASA grants NNX14AG461A and NNX09AW19A (Farouk et al.).
data_quality_notes: The conditions of FLEX-1268 differ between sources: the final report caption gives 3 atm and 12 % O2 - 50 % N2 - 29 % He (which sums to 91 %); Farouk et al. give 2.75 atm, 21 % O2, 29 % He, balance N2.
The pressure above which re-ignition cycles appear differs: about 2 atm in the final report, 1.25 atm in the 2024 paper. Pressures were tested at discrete levels, so neither is a resolved boundary.
The final report says all CFI data are yet to be fully analysed and gives preliminary, mostly qualitative observations (findings shown as figures, without tabulated values).
The final report writes 'n-dodecanol' and 'iso-dodecanol' in section 5.1; from the rest of the report these are typos for n-dodecane and iso-dodecane.
No diagnostic measures gas temperature directly; the 700 to 900 K range comes from FLEX, and warm and cool flame temperatures come from models.
Heat conducted through the tether fiber can promote re-ignition (Farouk et al.); the report's finding of little fiber effect applies to the cool-flame extinction diameter.
Models with current n-dodecane chemistry did not reproduce re-ignition and predicted a warm-flame stage about twice as long as measured.
In a 2 atm (1520 mmHg) cool-flame image the droplet was close to the edge of the field of view.
The report states that no new anomalies occurred; its 30-day operational report is marked 'not available'.
A third-party repository lists the DOI as 10.60555/m6pj-a914 (not verified).
key_results: Cool flames were observed for n-dodecane and for n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures; adding iso-dodecane reduced the tendency to form cool flames.

Warm flames appeared typically at higher pressures after radiative extinction, invisible on the color camera, followed by re-ignition of a hot flame that quickly goes out to form a cool flame. Helium appears to help the heat release and heat loss balance within the NTC region.

Above approximately 2 atm, multiple re-ignition cycles (hot flame, cool flame, hot flame again) were commonly observed until the droplet was fully consumed, which was unexpected from FLEX. A later peer-reviewed analysis places the onset of warm flames and re-ignitions above 1.25 atm.

Cool-flame extinction is controlled mainly by chemical kinetics: as the droplet shrinks, residence time falls until the cool flame becomes unstable. The 40-micrometer fiber had relatively little effect on the cool-flame extinction diameter of n-dodecane in air.
More helium led to earlier cool-flame extinction and a larger extinction diameter.

At low pressure a stable spherical soot shell formed during the hot flame and no soot formed during the cool flame; at higher pressure the soot shell became diffuse and unstable, and residual soot remained around the droplet after hot-flame extinction. The mechanisms are not understood.

At 1 atm and below, the cool-flame extinction diameter increases and the cool-flame burning rate decreases as pressure falls; at 5 atm the hot flame does not go out abruptly but dims gradually (Dietrich et al. 2024).

Modeling of these conditions gives about 1500 K for the hot flame, about 970 K for the warm flame and about 765 K for the cool flame (Farouk et al.); FLEX placed cool flames at 700 to 900 K against more than 1200 K for hot flames.
In FLEX, a vapor cloud formed around the droplet as partly oxidized fuel condensed right after cool-flame extinction.

record.name: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
record.approach: The P-Trak counts particles by condensing alcohol vapor onto them; the commercial condenser relies on gravity to return the liquid. NASA GRC's Microgravity Fluids Branch redesigned it to use capillary forces, and the mercury tilt switch was removed. Because of upmass limits the kit was split into DAFT-1 (modified P-Trak and wick), DAFT-2 (DustTrak), DAFT-3 (sample generation and filtering) and DAFT-4 (unmodified P-Trak, never used). In Increment 10, with no dust samples yet on board, both instruments sampled cabin air and Velcro-generated particles. In Increment 13 they sampled 15 L Mylar bags filled with Arizona Road Dust (Fine) dispersed by ISS nitrogen. Readings were voiced down every 30 s, and later checked against the instruments' memory after return to Earth.
record.conditions_note: ISS cabin atmosphere; no combustion. Oxygen and pressure not recorded in the reports.
record.flow: instrument pumps draw the sample; flow rates not given in the reports (the impactor was designed for the combined flow of both instruments)
record.geometry: hand-held instruments sampling cabin air through a shared sample port, or 15 L Mylar sample bags filled through a fill assembly (regulator, pressure relief valves, HEPA filter) and sampled through the DAFT impactor
record.gravity_note: ISS
record.hardware_note: Modified TSI P-Trak (P-Trak-01, launched on Progress 16P) with alcohol wick S/N 01; TSI DustTrak (launched on 16P) with a 2.5-micrometer impactor; DAFT fill assembly, DAFT impactor (removes large particles at only about 50 % efficiency), 15 L Mylar bags and dust holders each holding 0.25 g of Arizona Road Dust (Fine, a NIST standard), of which about 10 % (about 25 mg) is delivered. The unmodified P-Trak (P-Trak-02) launched on ULF1.1 but was never operated. P-Trak maximum count 500,000 pt/cc; the team considers its optimal range 30,000 to 100,000 pt/cc, and 20 to 80 mg/m3 for the DustTrak.
record.investigators_note: The PSI record lists David L. Urban as PI and Claire Fortenberry as project scientist (citation: Urban DL, Fortenberry C.). The final report lists David Urban and Gary Ruff (NASA GRC) as Principal Investigators, with co-authors William Sheredy (NASA GRC, project manager), Greg Funk and Nathan Funk (ZIN Technologies) and Zeng-guang Yuan (NCSER). The 30-day report lists David Urban as PI and George Mulholland (University of Maryland), Zeng-guang Yuan, Jiann Yang and Thomas Cleary (NIST) as Co-Investigators; Mulholland supplied the design criteria for the DAFT impactor. Crew: Leroy Chiao (Increment 10) and Jeffrey Williams (Increment 13).
record.objective: Reduce the risk to the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) by showing that the modified TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter works effectively and predictably in long-duration low gravity. The PSI record summarizes the objectives as: (1) demonstrate the functionality of the modified P-Trak in microgravity; (2) compare its performance against the DustTrak; (3) create and analyse aerosol standards in microgravity; (4) ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments. Secondary result: first measurement of particle levels in ISS cabin air.

record.funding: Built in answer to a NASA Headquarters call (March 2003, after the Columbia accident) for small experiments that could launch on Russian Progress vehicles within six months
record.hypothesis: Two failure modes were feared: (1) the counting optics would clog or be obscured by the isopropyl alcohol working fluid; (2) the flow inside the optics chamber would cause over-counting. The hypotheses were that the modified P-Trak would work normally in microgravity, and that the aerosol made and filtered per the design would be within the measuring range of both instruments.
data_quality_notes: The cabin air comparison in the reports is internally inconsistent: 2 to 5 pt/cc is called 'almost an order of magnitude' below a typical laboratory at about 4,000 to 6,000 pt/cc, which is about three orders of magnitude; elsewhere the same report says 'a factor of ten leaner than normal US office conditions'. During Increment 10 the readings never exceeded 20 % of the instruments' range, which the report says leaves those results 'somewhat suspect'.
The 0-g ratio (0.0024922) is exactly Bag 1's mean DustTrak/P-Trak ratio (43.15 / 17,314.3), so the 3.24 factor and the 1.48 diameter ratio rest on Bag 1 alone.

The report says the bag data were within the instruments' optimal ranges, but the P-Trak bag means (17,256 to 24,350 pt/cc) are below the 30,000 to 100,000 pt/cc it gives as optimal for the P-Trak; only the DustTrak means (34 to 63 mg/m3) are inside its 20 to 80 mg/m3 range.

Bag readings were not steady: in Bag 2 the P-Trak fell from 25,000 to 12,500 pt/cc while the DustTrak stayed at about 33 to 38 mg/m3, and Bag 3 ranged from 11,400 to 36,500 pt/cc. A falling count at steady mass is also what under-counting from low alcohol or optics build-up would produce, so the 'larger particles stay suspended' interpretation is not the only one.

The alcohol wick used (S/N 01) had been loaded more than 3 years earlier and was already used in Increment 10; wick S/N 02 could not be opened. The report describes the remaining alcohol as 'highly questionable'.
The P-Trak upper size limit differs between sources: DAFT reports say particles above 2.5 micrometers are above its measurement limit, while SAME papers give 20 nm to 1 micrometer.
The dust mass measured (34 to 63 mg/m3) is only about 2 to 4 % of the roughly 1.7 g/m3 expected if all 25 mg stayed suspended in 15 L; losses are not quantified.

Only 3 of 15 planned bags were run and the unmodified P-Trak control was never operated; the electronic data downlink failed, and the instrument memory read after return reproduced the voiced readings closely.
The more detailed discussion of low-alcohol readings and dust build-up is in SAME-RPT-019, 'DAFT Final Mission Test Report', which was not available.

The PSI record text has small errors: it calls the dust 'Arizona Red Dust' (it is Arizona Road Dust, Fine) and calls the DustTrak a 'CNC specifically designed to work in microgravity' (it is a light-scattering photometer, flown unmodified because it was judged gravity-insensitive).

The PSI experimental table lists sessions D1 (GMT 54, 2005) and D2 (GMT 63, 2005) with Arizona Road Dust as the sample, but no dust was on board then: those sessions sampled cabin air and Velcro particles. The table reports 3 rows; only D1 and D2 were visible in the saved page.
PSI-47 is Version 5 (updated 2 June 2025, 'additional documentation release'; 185 files removed, 32 added); total size 39.83 MB.
key_results: The modified P-Trak worked in microgravity for an extended time with no apparent failure: no alcohol build-up in the optics, no zero readings or error codes, and readings from zero up into the middle of its range and back. This retired a significant risk for SAME, which later flew in Increment 15 with the P-Traks working over the whole test matrix.

ISS cabin air was very clean: voiced readings of 2 to 5 pt/cc in the US Lab, attributed to the HEPA filters of the ISS air system. The report compares this with about 4,000 to 6,000 pt/cc in a typical laboratory and 'a factor of ten' below normal US office conditions.
Pulling Velcro apart produced P-Trak readings above 30,000 pt/cc, rising and falling in a logical way.

In the dust bags the count-to-mass ratio was lower than in ground calibration (flight DustTrak/P-Trak ratio 0.00249 against 0.00077 on the ground, a factor of 3.24, or 1.48 in equivalent diameter). The report attributes this to larger particles staying suspended without gravity and argues it rules out over-counting, one of the feared failure modes.
Mass per counted particle was 2.0 to 2.6 x 10^-12 g, an equivalent diameter of 1.56 to 1.70 micrometers if water density is assumed.

The report notes the count-to-mass ratio fell as P-Trak run time increased, especially in Bag 3, consistent with large dust particles building up in the optics chamber in lab tests; the P-Trak also began beeping before Bag 2, possibly a low-alcohol warning.

record.name: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets
record.approach: Raw Nikon NEF images from SPICE were decoded into three color channels and analysed by color-ratio pyrometry to obtain soot temperature fields; SPICE's absolute light calibration was then used to compute soot volume fractions. A coupled flow-species-soot model was modified to include radiation re-absorption and discrete-sectional aggregate formation, and run for both the Yale and ACME burner configurations in normal gravity and microgravity. Comparisons with the measurements guided sensitivity studies of soot parameters, including radiation, scattering, boundary conditions and heat transfer to the burner.

record.name: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
record.approach: A previously developed framework for fully coupled fluid-solid simulations of charring and ablating materials was extended with the unsteady FGM method and tested on BASS geometries: flat sheets, spheres and rods of PMMA, and wax cylinders. BASS and BASS-II images in PSI were post-processed with newly developed two-color tomography methods for DSLR cameras, giving 3-D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields to compare with the model. Evaluation metrics were flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Results were also compared with a parallel NSF-supported normal-gravity flame spread project.
record.conditions_note: Simulated and BASS test conditions are not given on the record.
record.flow: concurrent forced flow (flame spreading in the direction of the flow); velocities not given on the record
record.geometry: BASS sample geometries: flat sheets, spheres and rods of PMMA, and wax cylinders, in a concurrent flow

record.investigators_note: Citation on the PSI record: DesJardin P, Urban D. Proposal title is the same as the investigation title. Co-authors on the listed publications: Kenneth Budzinski and Siddhant S. Aphale. Comparisons were also made with a parallel NSF-supported normal-gravity flame spread project.
record.objective: Develop and validate unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) modeling for concurrent flame spread in microgravity, where heat transfer, mass transport and chemistry are tightly coupled near the solid surface and traditional hybrid turbulence-chemistry models are not fully consistent and miss intermediate reaction pathways. The UFGM approach maps the reacting system onto lower-dimensional manifolds to simulate solid fuel combustion with high fidelity, using the NASA BASS and BASS-II experiments as benchmarks. The long-term goal is to predict flammability limits of spacecraft materials and to provide a sub-grid model for large-eddy simulations of fires.

record.space_benefits: Predictive tools for screening the flammability limits of new materials, leading to safer spacecraft designs. Large-eddy simulation sub-grid models are expected to improve fire hazard assessment for long-duration missions and confined habitats.

record.hypothesis: The UFGM approach can accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.

record.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2
record.approach: The chamber was filled with the chosen atmosphere and left about 2 minutes to settle. Fuel was dispensed to form a droplet, free or on a support fiber; the needles retracted and at least 10 s passed for internal motion to die down. The igniters were powered for 1 to 5 s and retracted. In some tests the droplet was then moved at a steady slow speed to create a weak flow, and some tests used two droplets in a line.
record.conditions_note: Planned test matrix envelope (PSI experimental table and FLEX-2 SRD Table 2): O2 mole fraction 0.17, 0.21, 0.25 or 0.30 in nitrogen or helium, at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 or 3.0 atm. The SRD and Engineering Requirements Document (ERD) require the hardware to cover O2 0.10 to 0.40 (+/-0.005 on the initial charge) and 0.5 to 3.0 atm (+/-0.05 atm), with chamber pressure held within +/-10 % of the initial value during a test, initial gas and fuel temperature 18 to 27 C, relative humidity below 10 %, fuel vapor below 0.005 and each combustion product below 0.02 mole fraction before a test, and at least 2 minutes of settling after each chamber fill. Per-test values are not in the files read.
record.flow: Quiescent ambient in most tests; a controlled sub-buoyant convective flow was produced in some tests by translating the droplet at a uniform speed of 0.1–5 cm/s (motion starting when the igniters retract)
record.geometry: Isolated spherical droplets of 1.5 to 5 mm initial diameter (+/-0.25 mm, reproducible within 5 %), deployed between two opposed needles of 0.010 inch (0.25 mm) OD stainless steel tubing with flared tips, either released free or placed on a beaded support fiber. Fiber: 235 mm long, 79 micron diameter silicon carbide, tensioned between two arms, with small stainless steel beads every 12 mm to pin droplets; it is rotated 68 degrees into the deployment area and can be translated to make a slow flow or to deploy two droplets in a line 12 or 24 mm apart. Ignition by two opposed hot-wire igniters (4 mm loops of 30 AWG Kanthal A-1 wire), with dual-droplet igniter tips for the array tests; everything except the fiber is kept out of a sphere of 10 initial droplet diameters after ignition. Centre of the CIR combustion chamber.
record.gravity_note: ISS
record.hardware_note: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) chamber insert inside the CIR combustion chamber: two fuel dispensers (syringe, latching solenoid valve, stepper motor), needle deployment system, fiber support system, two igniters, cooling plate on ISS water, a two-radiometer package, a color camera and white LED lighting. Avionics on the CIR optics bench run the test sequence automatically and are commanded from the ground. CIR provides the chamber, gas mixing (FOMA) and the main cameras.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigators: Frederick L. Dryer (Princeton University), Benjamin D. Shaw (UC Davis), Mun Y. Choi (University of Connecticut), Vedha Nayagam (Case Western Reserve University), C. Thomas Avedisian (Cornell University), Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA GRC).
record.objective: Extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustors, and provide benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions to validate numerical simulations and develop new theoretical models. Detailed objectives: (1) role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning of bi-component droplets; (2) steady and unsteady liquid- and gas-phase phenomena in pure-fuel combustion; (3) flame extinction mechanisms and boundaries; (4) soot formation, including soot volume fraction and soot-shell dynamics; (5) influence of droplet interactions on flammability limits and extinction of droplet arrays; (6) validation of droplet-combustion models.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: Planned oxygen from 17 to 30 % and pressures from 0.5 to 3 atm, with nitrogen or helium. Conditions cannot be tied to individual tests from the files read. The fuel is a liquid droplet, so it informs models rather than solid material selection.
record.space_benefits: FLEX-2 is aimed mainly at the fundamental understanding of liquid-fuel combustion rather than at fire safety (unlike FLEX), but its SRD notes that microgravity droplet combustion is of direct concern for combustion hazards in spacecraft for human exploration. Its extinction, soot and radiation data support fire models for spacecraft.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with numerical simulations
record.earth_benefits: Liquid fuels are the main energy source for transport. Benchmark data on realistic and multi-component fuels support cleaner, more efficient combustors and the evaluation of future fuels.
record.hypothesis: Numerical simulations of droplet combustion make approximations for chemistry, radiation and the coupling of gas and liquid that have not been checked against benchmark data. Microgravity removes buoyancy, so the droplet behavior depends only on capillary stresses and the basic processes, including the change from radiative to diffusive extinction, can be observed and compared with the models.

record.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
record.approach: Single droplets of methanol or n-heptane were deployed in the CIR chamber, free or on a thin fiber, and ignited by hot wires. For each pressure the oxygen level was lowered and the droplet size varied until the flame either burned to completion, extinguished at a finite droplet size, or failed to ignite, which gives the limiting oxygen index. The tests were repeated with CO2 or helium added. In some tests the droplet was moved slowly near the end of the burn to add a weak flow. The 2005 requirements document planned the tests as sub-matrices: limiting oxygen index (LOI) versus pressure for heptane and methanol in still and slowly flowing gas, then the efficacy of CO2, helium and SF6 over a range of pressures and oxygen levels, the effect of a slow flow on CO2 efficacy, and the effect of higher pressure (stronger radiation) on suppressant efficacy.
record.conditions_note: Per-test initial ambient composition and pressure from the PSI experimental table (274 tests). Most tests were near 0.7 atm or 1 atm; 9 tests were at about 2 to 3 atm, all at 21 % O2. The balance gas is nitrogen, with CO2 up to 70 % or helium up to 45 % in the suppressant tests. The 2005 requirements document asked for O2 0.10 to 0.40 (+/-0.005), suppressants CO2, He and SF6 from 0 to 0.7 mole fraction, nitrogen as the balance, 0.5 to 3.0 atm (+/-0.05 atm, held within +/-10 % during a test), initial gas and fuel temperature 18 to 27 C, and relative humidity below 10 % for heptane and below 2 % for methanol. No SF6 tests appear in the PSI table. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is a nominal value (cabin room temperature, about 25 °C), assumed by the team; it was not measured or reported for these tests.
record.flow: Quiescent (no forced flow); some tests imposed a small sub-buoyant convective flow by slowly translating the droplet near the end of burning, and free droplets could have a small residual drift velocity
record.geometry: Isolated spherical droplets, initial diameter 1.1–4.67 mm, deployed between two opposed 250 µm OD stainless-steel needles that retract before ignition (free droplets) or onto an 80 µm SiC support fiber (fiber-supported droplets), at the center of the CIR combustion chamber (~90 L); hot-wire igniters retracted after ignition
record.gravity_note: ISS, with supporting ground-based tests
record.hardware_note: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus inside the Combustion Integrated Rack chamber (about 90 L, rated to about 9 atm). Droplets are formed between two 250 micron needles that retract before ignition, or on an 80 micron SiC fiber. The CIR gas system (FOMA) sets the atmosphere.

record.objective: Map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity, measure the effectiveness of gaseous fire suppressants (e.g. CO2, He), and develop and validate predictive models of combustion and extinction limits under reduced gravity, using high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction, flame radiation, soot and temperature over a systematic range of ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations.

The fuel is a liquid droplet, so it informs limits and models rather than solid material selection.
record.space_benefits: Flammability limits and suppressant effectiveness in microgravity, relevant to choosing spacecraft atmospheres and fire suppressants (the ISS uses CO2 extinguishers), and benchmark data for fire models.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with ground tests and numerical models
record.earth_benefits: Better droplet combustion models and understanding of cool-flame chemistry, relevant to engine efficiency and emissions.
record.hypothesis: Without buoyant convection, the transport of heat and species, radiative heat loss and chemical kinetics all change, so the flammability limits of liquid fuels and the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants differ from those in normal gravity.

record.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
record.approach: The Saffire-I module (flow duct plus avionics bay) flew on the Cygnus OA-6 cargo vehicle and was operated from the ground about a day after Cygnus left the ISS in June 2016. One large SIBAL fabric sample (about 0.4 m x 0.94 m) on a metal frame sat in the middle of a 46 x 51 cm flow duct; fans at the top drew cabin air through flow straighteners at the bottom at 20 cm/s. A hot-wire igniter woven across the sample started test 1 (concurrent flow, ignition at the upstream bottom edge) for an allotted 420 s; the flow was then stopped and restarted, and test 2 (opposed flow, ignition at the top) ran as a contingency on the remaining fuel. Two cameras recorded the flame, with radiometers, thermocouples and O2, CO2 and pressure sensors. All data were compressed and downlinked (maximum 20 Gbit) before Cygnus re-entered and burned up.
record.conditions_note: O2 from the PSI experimental table: 21.5–21.7 % for test 1 (concurrent) and about 21.5 % for test 2 (opposed); the published starting value is 21.7 %. The fire consumed about 1.5 % of the vehicle's oxygen. Pressure and temperature are measured values from the Cygnus pressurized cargo module (PCM) sensors in the PSI file 'Saffire-I Telemetry Data Good Process Version.xlsx': pressure 14.47–14.54 psi and air temperature 19.67–20.18 °C (292.8–293.3 K) over the test period; ambient_temperature_K is the mid-range value.
record.flow: Forced, uniform air flow of 20 cm/s through the 46 x 51 cm duct, drawn by fans at the top after flow straighteners at the bottom. Test 1: concurrent (flame spreading with the flow). Test 2: opposed (flame spreading against the flow). The flow was turned off after test 1 and restarted after 210 s for test 2.
record.geometry: Single large thin fabric sample, 94 cm long x 40.6 cm wide, about 0.37 mm thick, on a metal frame in the center of a rectangular flow duct with a 46 x 51 cm cross-section; the flame spread along the sample (two-sided burning). The fiberglass matrix kept the sample intact after the cotton burned.
record.gravity_note: Free-flying Cygnus cargo vehicle in low Earth orbit after leaving the ISS (June 2016); compared with normal-gravity behavior, where upward flames over a sample of this size accelerate and grow
record.hardware_note: Saffire-I flight unit inside the Cygnus pressurized cargo module: flow duct (46 x 51 cm) with the sample card, fans and flow straighteners, hot-wire igniter (29-gage Kanthal, 0.286 mm, 3.85 A, saw-tooth pattern), two digital video cameras, four radiometers, six thermocouples, O2, CO2 and pressure sensors, two anemometers, and an avionics bay. The unit was destroyed on re-entry, so all data were downlinked.

The specific objective of Saffire-I (and Saffire-III) was to determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate.

record.space_benefits: First data on a realistic-scale fire in a spacecraft cabin: flame growth, spread rate, limiting flame size and heat release rate in microgravity, used to validate fire models, NASA's material selection criteria and the design of fire detection and suppression for exploration vehicles.

data_quality_notes: The investigation start and end dates on the PSI page (2 March 2001 and 28 February 2008) and its proposal title ('Characterization of Smoke from Microgravity Fires for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection') belong to another investigation, not to Saffire-I (flown in 2016), so start_date and end_date were left null.
PSI lists the flight program as ISS, but the experiment ran in the Cygnus vehicle after it left the ISS.
The PSI table swaps sample length and width (length 40.6, width 94 cm) and gives the thickness as 0.37 cm; the published sample is 94 cm long x 40.6 cm wide, and SIBAL fabric is about 0.37 mm thick.
Test 2 (opposed) was a contingency run on the roughly 10 % of fuel left after test 1, so it was brief.
Telemetry was not available during operations, so both tests ran on a timer whether or not a flame was present.
No project scientist is listed on the PSI page.

Pressure and ambient temperature come from the Cygnus PCM sensors (CygnusPressureData and CygnusTemperatureData sheets of 'Saffire-I Telemetry Data Good Process Version.xlsx'); these are cabin readings, not readings inside the Saffire flow duct.
key_results: First intentionally set large-scale fire inside an orbiting spacecraft, an order of magnitude larger than any earlier microgravity sample.

In concurrent flow the flame, after an ignition transient, reached a steady length of about 40 mm and spread at about 1.8 mm/s (about 1.5 kW), burning about 90 % of the sample; in normal gravity an upward flame over a sample this size accelerates and grows.
In opposed flow the flame was shorter (about 24 mm) and slower (about 1.3 mm/s, about 1.1 kW); at 20 cm/s concurrent spread was clearly faster than opposed spread.
Flame spread was slower than in earlier microgravity tests in smaller ducts, showing that confinement and scale affect flame behavior.
The fire consumed about 1.5 % of the oxygen available in the vehicle.
A limiting flame size can be used to set the heat release rate for spacecraft design; the authors argue that rating materials only with normal-gravity tests needs revised assumptions.
