record.name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
record.approach: The Saffire-II module (flow duct plus avionics bay) flew on the Cygnus OA-5 cargo vehicle and was operated from the ground after Cygnus left the ISS on 21 November 2016. A sample card with 9 samples (5 cm x 29 cm each) sat in the middle of a large flow duct; fans at the top of the duct drew cabin air through flow straighteners at the bottom. The samples were ignited one after another with a hot-wire igniter at the upstream end (concurrent flow) or downstream end (opposed flow) and burned in forced air flow of 20 cm/s (PSI table; the PSI summary mentions 20 or 30 cm/s). Two cameras recorded the flames, and thermocouples, radiometers, O2, CO2 and pressure sensors and anemometers recorded the conditions. All data were compressed and downlinked (maximum 20 Gbit) before Cygnus re-entered and burned up on 27 November 2016.
record.conditions_note: O2 values come from the PSI experimental table: about 21.5 % for sample 1 and about 22.1 % for the others, dropping to 21.9 % by the end of sample 9. They were derived from the measured CO2 production and referenced to the initial O2 reported by the ISS. Pressure and temperature are measured values from the Cygnus pressurized cargo module (PCM) sensors in the PSI file 'Saffire-II Telemetry Data.xlsx': pressure 14.56–14.64 psi and air temperature 19.78–21.33 °C (292.9–294.5 K) over the test period; ambient_temperature_K is the mid-range value.
record.flow: Forced air flow drawn through the flow duct by fans at the top, after flow straighteners at the bottom. 20 cm/s for all nine samples in the PSI table (the PSI summary says 20 or 30 cm/s depending on material; a 2017 paper reports the two SIBAL samples at 20 and 25 cm/s). Concurrent flow for 8 samples and opposed flow for sample 4 (silicone). The design range was 10–30 cm/s. Flow was turned off at the end of some burns.
record.geometry: Nine thin or thick flat solid samples, each 5 cm wide x 29 cm long, mounted on one sample card (3 x 3 layout) in the middle of the Saffire flow duct; flames spread along the sample surfaces (two-sided burning). Thicknesses: silicone 0.27–1.03 mm, SIBAL fabric about 0.37 mm, PMMA 10 mm with a tapered edge for ignition, structured PMMA 10 mm with a 4 mm grooved center, PMMA 0.85 mm followed by Nomex 0.37 mm. The overall Saffire module was about 53 x 90 x 133 cm.
record.gravity_note: Free-flying Cygnus cargo vehicle in low Earth orbit after leaving the ISS (21 November 2016); compared with normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 results and ground tests (e.g., UC Berkeley low-pressure tests, ZARM Bremen)
record.hardware_note: Saffire-II flight unit inside the Cygnus pressurized cargo module: flow duct with sample card, fans and flow straighteners, hot-wire igniters, two cameras, thermocouples, radiometers, solid-state O2, CO2 and pressure sensors, two anemometers, and an avionics bay with power, computer and data acquisition. Both SIBAL fabric samples burned completely (29 cm) with spread rates of 2.1 and 2.6 mm/s; in microgravity the concurrent flame reached a nearly steady length instead of accelerating as in normal gravity.

The thick PMMA flames reached a steady limiting length and stayed anchored at the upstream end, so flame spread is controlled by the slow regression rate (0.01–0.04 mm/s); a grooved center section formed a deep inverted-V notch that increased heat transfer.
Flames went out quickly when the flow was turned off, supporting the ISS strategy of shutting off ventilation on a fire alarm.
A limiting flame size in low-speed forced flow makes flashover in a spacecraft unlikely and can be used to set the heat release rate for vehicle design.
Normal-gravity tests at reduced pressure approximate the microgravity spread rates (about 30 kPa for the SIBAL fabric).
All nine samples burned as planned and all data were downlinked by 25 November 2016 (complete mission success).

record.name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
record.approach: Reused the SAME hardware already on orbit. Small material samples were heated by a wire for about 60 s to produce smoke without flame; the smoke was measured immediately and again after aging in a chamber. Changes from SAME: Pyrell foam replaced the dibutyl-phthalate samples; higher heating temperatures and a no-flow condition were added; the MPASS instrument replaced one diagnostic enclosure. Flight tests ran from 16 July to 9 September 2010 (66 test points). Three post-flight ground tests followed: flow tests for dilution ratios, 1 g microscope samples under the same conditions, and size-distribution measurements to check the lognormal assumption.
record.conditions_note: Oxygen and pressure were not test variables and are not stated in the metadata, table or final report; tests ran in the Microgravity Science Glovebox in ISS cabin air. Note: relevant to fire detection in any crewed vehicle or habitat; oxygen and pressure were not varied, so it says nothing specific about the lunar-base atmosphere. The dust-versus-smoke discrimination result is relevant to dusty lunar and Martian habitats.
record.space_benefits: Baseline low-gravity smoke data for evaluating current spacecraft smoke detectors and for designing an advanced fire detector for long-duration missions.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with post-flight ground tests
record.earth_benefits: Smoke detectors based on these results can be used in other confined, extreme environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories.
record.hypothesis: Without buoyant flow, smoke from a pyrolyzing or smoldering source stays longer and more concentrated near the source, so particles grow larger than in normal gravity (with fewer particles for the same smoke mass). This changes how smoke detectors respond and could leave some detectors without an alarm.
diluents: nitrogen (used only to dilute the smoke stream for the instruments)
data_quality_notes: The experiment table gives dates without a year (the final report gives 2010).
Test 57 appears under both Lampwick and Teflon with the same values; one of the two rows is probably a duplicate entry.
The final report is a working document: it reuses text from a conference paper and has an unresolved reference marker ('ref. xx').
key_results: Smoke particle size depends strongly on the material. Teflon and Kapton smoke particles are very small (diameter of average mass about 0.1 to 0.17 micrometers unaged); lamp wick, silicone and Pyrell are several times larger.

The small Teflon and Kapton particles are hard to detect with light-scattering detectors, while a detector sensitive enough for them would give nuisance alarms from large dust particles. The report concludes that reliable detection needs a detector measuring more than one moment of the size distribution.

The MPASS two-moment sensor gave a response at least twice as uniform across materials and particle sizes as a single-output sensor, and can tell a high smoke concentration from a lower concentration of large dust particles, reducing false alarms.
Particles grow as smoke ages: for most materials the diameters roughly doubled after 720 s.

Particles are larger at low airflow. With no flow during heating, the diameter of average mass was 30 to 40 % larger for all materials. Smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can therefore be expected to be much larger than smoke released in ventilated areas. This effect is specific to low gravity.
Smoke from lamp wick, silicone rubber and Kapton forms liquid droplets; Teflon and Pyrell form solid, chain-like agglomerates. Pyrell changed to spherical particles under no flow.
The moment method with a lognormal size distribution was validated by the flight and ground tests as a way to characterize spacecraft smoke.
Unlike SAME, the electron microscope samples were clean and gave good particle images.

record.name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
record.approach: Small samples (about 3 mm diameter cylinders of material wrapped in a stainless steel wire) were resistively heated below their ignition point for about 60 s, with wire resistance used to control temperature; samples were pre-weighed and loaded six to a carousel. A piston drew the smoke over the sample at 2 to 8 cm/s into an aging chamber, held it for 10 to 1800 s to let particles coagulate, then pushed it past three instruments that each measure a different moment of the size distribution, plus ISS and Space Shuttle smoke detectors and a thermal precipitator collecting particles on TEM grids. Assuming a lognormal distribution, the moments give mean diameters and the spread of sizes. Samples were run at different temperatures, flows and aging times. Operated mostly from the ground, which allowed about 50 % more test points than planned. An FDS model simulated smoke transport and detector response in the ISS US Lab.
record.conditions_note: Pyrolysis in air inside the glovebox; oxygen and pressure values not given in the report. No flaming combustion.
record.flow: air flow over the sample of 2 to 8 cm/s, induced by the moving piston of the aging chamber during heating
record.geometry: small cylindrical samples heated in a smoke generation duct, with an aging chamber and a diagnostics duct, inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox
record.gravity_note: ISS
record.hardware_note: Moment instruments: capillary-modified TSI P-Trak (zeroth moment, number concentration, 0 to 10^5 pt/cc and 20 nm to 1 micrometer, dilution needed since smoke reached 0.5 to 5 x 10^6 pt/cc); ionization chamber from a residential smoke detector (first moment, diameter concentration, no dilution); two TSI DustTraks with 1-micrometer and 10-micrometer inlet impactors (third moment, mass, 0.001 to 100 mg/m3; their difference gives the fraction above 1 micrometer). Signals digitized at 1 Hz by an 8-bit A/D converter. Calibrated before flight with monodisperse dioctyl phthalate droplets and polystyrene spheres against a TSI 3022 counter, a TEOM and a TSI Electrical Aerosol Detector. For the final results the DustTrak was calibrated directly for each smoke source against TEOM mass measurements, and estimated material densities were used to compute the diameter of average mass. About 5 hours of crew time to assemble.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigator: Jiann C. Yang (NIST). Final report authors: David L. Urban, Gary A. Ruff and William Sheredy (NASA GRC), Thomas Cleary and Jiann Yang (NIST), George Mulholland (University of Maryland) and Zeng-Guang Yuan (NCSER). John E. Brooker (NASA GRC) built the transport model; Victoria Bryg (NCSER) co-authored the 2009 analysis.
record.objective: Characterize the size distribution of smoke particles produced in low gravity by overheated spacecraft materials, including how aging and coagulation change it on the way to a detector, so that next-generation smoke detectors can be designed for exploration missions.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: pyrolysis smoke from real spacecraft materials in ISS air; oxygen and pressure were not varied, so the tests do not cover lunar base atmospheres. Directly relevant to fire detection, including the need to reject lunar dust, rather than to flammability.
record.space_benefits: First smoke particle size data from overheated spacecraft materials in low gravity, used to set design requirements for future spacecraft smoke detectors. The report notes that extended lunar-surface missions will need detectors not fooled by lunar and other nuisance dust; telling smoke from dust (which tends to be large) will probably require some discrimination of particle size.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with ground calibration, normal-gravity comparison tests and a CFD smoke transport model
record.earth_benefits: Smoke detector design for other closed environments, such as submarines and underwater laboratories.

record.fuel_state: solid (and one liquid held on a wick)

fuel: dibutyl phthalate (DBP) retained in a cotton wick, used as a reference
data_quality_notes: Size values come from three analysis stages that should not be mixed: count mean diameters from two instruments (2008), interim three-moment values (AIAA-2009-956, e.g. Teflon Dg 159 nm, silicone not converged) and the final report's Table 1 (Teflon Dg 170 nm). The final arithmetic means (257, 205, 227, 105 nm) are 2 to 9 % below the 2008 count means (263, 223, 248, 114 nm).
The final Table 1 is internally consistent with a lognormal distribution: Dg * exp(0.5 ln^2 sigma_g) and Dg * exp(1.5 ln^2 sigma_g) reproduce the arithmetic mean and D1.5 within rounding.

Two statements in the final report's text contradict its own Table 1: it calls 189 nm the 'count mean diameter' of silicone (Table 1 gives 189 nm as the geometric mean and 257 nm as the arithmetic mean), and it says the aged silicone diameter of average mass rises 'to over 1 micrometer' (Table 1 gives 606 nm; the 2009 ICES paper says 'over 500 nm').
The percentage increases over normal gravity come from the 2008 paper and are given without the 1-g reference diameters, sample sizes or uncertainties.

The 30 samples were run at different flow, temperature and aging conditions (47 test points in all), so there are few or no replicates per exact condition, and Table 1 gives single values per material without stating which runs they come from.
The report gives formulas for propagating moment uncertainties (M1 contributes most, M3 least) but no uncertainty values for the Table 1 diameters.
DBP was tested 22 times as a reference material, but no DBP results are reported.

The moment method assumes spherical particles and a lognormal distribution; the DustTrak response depends strongly on particle size and refractive index, and the final values rely on a per-source TEOM calibration that holds only if the size distribution does not change much.
TEM grids were contaminated with particles from the thermal precipitator assembly, limiting microscopic checks.
The erratic ISS detector signal is documented for Teflon; for Kapton the difficulty is an inference from particle size.
key_results: For the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles were below 500 nm in diameter.

Teflon and Kapton smoke had small particles and narrow size distributions, with little mass above 1 micrometer. Silicone rubber and lamp wick smoke had much larger diameters of average mass, with almost half the mass in particles above 1 micrometer.

Aging the smoke for 720 s cut the number concentration while mass stayed fairly steady, consistent with coagulation with limited wall loss; the diameter of average mass grew (for example 179 to 267 nm for Kapton, 472 to 606 nm for silicone).
An earlier analysis found count mean diameters in low gravity typically about 50 % larger than in comparable normal-gravity tests (53 % silicone, 65 % lamp wick, 58 % Kapton).

All tests gave strong signals on the Space Shuttle ionization detector. For Teflon smoke, mostly below 1 micrometer, the ISS light-scattering detector signal was erratic. The authors conclude that small Kapton and Teflon particles are hard for light-scattering detectors while large silicone and lamp wick particles give very large signals, so detection against background dust needs a system that measures more than one moment of the size distribution.
The earlier CSD shuttle experiment saw poor Shuttle-detector response for overheated cellulose and silicone, which suggests some pre-fire conditions produce larger particles than SAME saw.

The FDS model showed smoke is mixed through the US Lab rather than collecting at the ceiling, so detection takes longer than in normal gravity; alarm times depend strongly on source location and obstructions, and some sources at the lowest soot yield never triggered an alarm.

record.name: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
record.approach: Crew-operated glovebox experiment using the SPICE hardware already on the ISS. For each test the crewmember installed a burner tube and a fuel bottle, set the fuel flow and fan (coflow) voltage, ignited the flame with a hot-wire igniter, then varied the fuel flow or the air coflow as directed live from the ground (Telescience Support Center at NASA GRC) and took bracketed high-resolution still photographs at each condition. Typically the fuel flow was fixed and the coflow raised slowly towards liftoff, after which the flame lifted and stabilized downstream or blew out; some tests held the coflow fixed and increased the fuel flow. Burns lasted about 1 minute and the glovebox was flushed with cabin air after every two burns. Fan calibrations (coflow velocity versus fan voltage) were run every test day, and pyrometry calibrations with flame-heated ceramic fibers were run on three days to allow absolute soot volume fraction measurements. Liftoff and blowout limits come from the video; flame structure, soot temperature and soot volume fraction come from the still photographs. About a quarter of the 2012 tests were for SPICE.
record.conditions_note: Nominal values, not measured per test. The final report states that the SLICE atmosphere was about 21 % O2 (by volume) with a balance of nitrogen and about 100 kPa (14.5 psi), i.e., MSG working volume filled with ISS cabin air. The SRD asked for the cabin O2 concentration and MSG pressure to be known when possible (MCA / Columbus sensors, CSA-CP, MSG differential pressure transducers), but there was no SLICE instrumentation for them. Testing was not allowed during thruster firings or dockings. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is a nominal value (cabin room temperature, about 25 °C), assumed by the team; it was not measured or reported for these tests.
record.flow: Forced coflow of air: ambient air from the MSG working volume is drawn by a fan, passes a flow straightener, the duct, an air velocity probe and a screen, flows past the burner tube, through a heat sink and out through a filtered soot trap. The coflow was set by the fan voltage (the probe response was too slow during tests) and calibrated each day. The published microgravity methane flames have average (fuel) inlet velocities of 23–90 cm/s. A reference coflow velocity of about 43 cm/s at full fan voltage is reported for March 2012. Fuel flow set by a mass flow controller (500 sccm full scale, N2 basis).
record.geometry: Round laminar gas-jet (coflow) diffusion flame issuing from an interchangeable straight stainless-steel burner tube on the axis of a fan-driven flow duct with a 76.2 mm square cross-section (rounded corners), with top and front windows. Burner tubes: nominal inner diameters 0.4, 0.8, 1.6, 2.1 and 3.2 mm (measured 0.4064–0.4191, 0.7620–0.7747, 1.5875–1.6002, 2.1336–2.1463 and 3.2258–3.2385 mm); the 2.1 and 3.2 mm tubes were added for SLICE. Flames attached to the tube or lifted and stabilized downstream.
record.gravity_note: ISS (MSG, Expedition 30), compared with normal-gravity tests on the ground unit (ELF/SPICE ground hardware) at Yale University and NASA GRC
record.hardware_note: SPICE experiment module (based on the ELF hardware) in the Microgravity Science Glovebox: fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes and hot-wire igniters, 12 fuel bottles (210 psia, 110 psia for propane), mass flow controller, Nikon D300s digital SLR (blackbody-characterized, optional BG-7 filter), analog video camera with data overlay, radiometer, thin-filament pyrometry fiber arrays on an alternate top window (BASS sample fixture), power/video box and external control box. New for SLICE: 2.1 and 3.2 mm burner tubes, D300s camera, new top window and fiber arrays.
record.investigators_note: PSI roles: Principal Investigator Marshall B. Long (Yale University); Co-Investigators Mitchell D. Smooke (Yale University) and Fumiaki Takahashi (Case Western Reserve University; NCSER at NASA GRC at the time); Project Scientist Dennis P. Stocker (NASA GRC), who was also a Co-Investigator and directed the crew. The final report also lists Robert W. Hawersaat (NASA GRC, Project Manager), Jay C. Owens (imaging), Tibor Lorik and Charles T. Bunnell (ZIN Technologies, development, training and operations), Carol L. Reynolds (NASA MSFC, Payload Operations Lead) and Bin Ma (Yale, data analysis and 1g tests, Ph.D.). The experiment was run on orbit by astronaut Don Pettit. Computational modeling by Su (Andy) Cao and Beth Anne V. Bennett (Yale). In 2017 NASA selected Takahashi to continue the analysis under a 2-year project, 'Structure and Stabilization of Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames'.
record.objective: Improve understanding of the physical and chemical processes that control the structure and lifting (stabilization) of non-premixed coflow flames, and provide rigorous tests of numerical models including thermal radiation, soot formation and detailed chemical kinetics. Specific objectives, for flames of methane, ethylene and selected nitrogen dilutions burning in a coflow of air: (1) characterize the flame structure, especially its base (stabilizing region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of fuel, burner diameter and flow conditions; (2) identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of fuel and burner diameter. A third objective (hysteresis of lifting and reattachment) was dropped a year before flight because the fuel supply was insufficient. SLICE was a precursor to the ACME Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment in the CIR.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: Gas jet flames in cabin air near 1 atm only; no variation of oxygen or pressure. It informs flame stability, liftoff and soot behavior rather than material flammability.
record.space_benefits: The research was aimed at Earth combustion, but the final report notes that SLICE results could plausibly help space technologies such as spacecraft fire safety or waste processing. It is also a precursor that reduced risk and improved the test matrix of the ACME CLD Flame experiment on the ISS.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with normal-gravity tests on the ground unit and numerical simulations (MC-Smooth vorticity-velocity model with sectional soot model)
record.earth_benefits: Data to validate coflow diffusion flame models over a wider range of conditions than possible in normal gravity, leading to better design tools for more efficient, lower-emission combustion devices (engines, industrial burners), and better understanding of soot formation and flame stability.
record.hypothesis: The structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are strongly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity and fuel composition and are fundamentally different from flames on Earth. The 30-day report states that the computational flame model of Smooke et al. effectively served as the hypothesis, and that higher forced velocities were expected to be needed to lift microgravity flames because there is no buoyant convection.
data_quality_notes: O2 and pressure were not measured: 21 % O2 and about 100 kPa (14.5 psi) are the nominal values stated in the final report.

Coflow velocity has significant uncertainty: fan calibrations varied from day to day (on 9 Feb 2012 up to 10 cm/s higher), the flow decreased as soot built up, and on the last day the reference velocity fell from about 43 to 9 cm/s after tests beyond the smoke point.

Lifted flames were always tilted, indicating an asymmetric coflow, probably from a duct screen found dislodged at set-up or air leakage at the duct door. Tilt is acceptable only near the burner (within about 1 cm).
Video data overlay anomaly at set-up (discharged titler battery); recovered on 6 Feb 2012 with a crew procedure before testing started.

start_date is the month NASA selected SLICE for flight development (July 2009); the PSI page has no start or end date. Operations ended 23 March 2012, but the final report (2017) says data analysis was still under way.
total_tests (about 120 ignitions) includes the SPICE tests run in 2012.
The HDR imaging paper (Applied Optics 54(14), 2015) is listed in the final report, not on the PSI page; its DOI was not checked.
ambient_temperature_K = 298 is nominal (assumed), not a measurement.
key_results: The 12 fuel bottles were fully consumed in 13 test days: about 120 ignitions and over 4,000 photographs at roughly 700 flame conditions.
Without buoyancy, microgravity flames are wider and less likely to lift off than in normal gravity, and more highly diluted flames can be stabilized.

Microgravity flames have lower soot temperatures (about 200 K lower) and soot volume fractions about an order of magnitude higher than their 1g counterparts, because of longer soot residence time. Soot shifts from the centerline to the flame wings.

Luminous flame length is proportional to the fuel mixture mass flow rate in both gravities; nonbuoyant flames are longer. Flame structure is mainly controlled by the fuel mass flow rate, with dilution and inlet velocity secondary (methane flames, CH4 mole fraction 0.4–1.0, inlet velocity 23–90 cm/s).
Microgravity flames were more resistant to lifting than expected, so later tests used smaller burner tubes to reach higher jet velocities.
The CH* concentration integrated over a cross-section scales with the computed heat release rate, and peak CH* differs little between 0g and 1g.
Numerical results (MC-Smooth model) agree well with the measurements of flame shape and soot temperature.

record.name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
record.approach: A gas jet flame was lit on a small nozzle on the centerline of a flow duct in the Microgravity Science Glovebox. For each fuel and nozzle the crew set the air speed with a fan, ignited the flame and adjusted the fuel flow by hand until the flame just began to emit soot (the smoke point). Crew and ground identified smoke points live on video; the video was analyzed afterwards for flame length. Typical burns lasted 60 s and the glovebox was flushed with cabin air after every two burns.
record.conditions_note: Not measured per test. The final report states that the ISS cabin air used to flush the glovebox is kept within 19 to 24 % O2 (a 2011 paper estimates 20 to 23 %). 101 kPa (14.65 psi), 298 K and 21 +/- 1 % O2 are the values assumed in the published calculations. The SRD specified only 'Shuttle ambient pressure'; oxygen was not a requirement. ambient_temperature_K = 298 is the value assumed in the published calculations, not a measurement.
record.flow: Forced co-flowing air from a 3-inch DC fan (Panasonic FBA08A12H1A) drawing on the glovebox atmosphere, through a ceramic honeycomb and screens to remove swirl; fan speed set by a multi-turn potentiometer (a minimum fan voltage is kept even at dial 0 so fuel cannot accumulate). Co-flow velocity 5.4–65 cm/s at the smoke points (table range up to ~85 cm/s). The duct velocity profile is non-uniform (lower on the centerline near the nozzle because of the nozzle boundary layer); it was mapped at 18 locations (stations 13 and 56 mm downstream of the nozzle tip) for 6 fan settings. Fuel flow set manually with a second potentiometer to cross the smoke point; typical burn 60 s, MSG flushed with ISS cabin air after every two burns.
record.geometry: Round laminar gas-jet diffusion flame issuing from one of three interchangeable stainless nozzles, all 50 mm long with inner diameters of 0.41 (0.4064), 0.76 (0.762) or 1.6 (1.6002) mm, mounted on the centerline of a rectangular flow duct with Lexan top and front windows. The final report gives the duct interior as 172 mm x 43 mm x 43 mm, while the papers and thesis describe an approximately 76 x 76 mm square cross-section with rounded corners. Nozzle tip ~54 mm downstream of the inlet screen (papers: screen 50 mm upstream); perforated copper plate 120 mm downstream followed by a copper screen and heat sink. Coiled Kanthal hot-wire igniter (~4 A) swung to the nozzle tip for ignition; 105 mm retractable 45°-tilted ruler for length calibration.
record.gravity_note: ISS, with normal-gravity tests on a prototype module at the University of Maryland
record.hardware_note: Flow duct apparatus modified from the Enclosed Laminar Flames (ELF) experiment, with a fan, three interchangeable nozzles (0.41, 0.76, 1.6 mm), hot-wire igniter, 12 exchangeable fuel bottles, mass flow controller, radiometer, still camera and video camera, operated with a hand-held control box.

Sunderland (University of Maryland, Co-Investigator), Zeng-Guang Yuan (National Center for Space Exploration Research, Project Scientist), Robert Hawersaat (NASA GRC, Glovebox Program Manager). Original principal investigator: Gerard M. Faeth (University of Michigan), until his death. Keenan T. Dotson (University of Maryland) analyzed the flight data for his M.S. thesis. ISS crew operators: Michael Barratt, E. Michael Fincke, Sandra H. Magnus, Koichi Wakata.
record.objective: Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity; determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on luminous flame lengths and smoke points; quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels (ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene/nitrogen mixtures); validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time; and investigate the effect of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke-point phenomena.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: Gas jet flames in cabin air near 1 atm only; no variation of oxygen or pressure. It informs soot and smoke behavior rather than material selection.
record.space_benefits: Understanding soot formation and emission in microgravity flames supports spacecraft fire safety strategies for long missions.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), with normal-gravity tests and an analytical residence-time model
record.earth_benefits: Smoke points measure a fuel's tendency to soot; better understanding of soot in laminar flames helps with soot in practical turbulent flames, which affects health, climate and fire spread.
record.funding: NASA: NNX07AO91A (cooperative agreement with the University of Maryland, per the 30-day report and the Dotson thesis)
record.hypothesis: Smoke-point behavior will be observed for flames in co-flowing air, and it will depend on nozzle diameter and co-flow velocity. With gravity-driven transport removed, flame properties are expected to differ from those in normal gravity.

diluents: nitrogen (in the fuel, for the propylene mixtures)
data_quality_notes: O2: the final report states that the ISS cabin air used to flush the MSG is maintained within 19–24% O2 (the 2011 paper estimated 20–23%); O2 was not measured per test. Calculations assume 21±1% O2.
Pressure was not measured: 101 kPa (14.65 psi) is the value assumed in the published calculations, so pressure_min_psi = pressure_max_psi = 14.65 is nominal.

In-flight anomaly: soot accumulated on the duct outlet screen and changed the coflow; the crew vacuumed it clean on 2009-06-15. This made propylene smoke points with the 0.41 mm burner non-repeatable between days.
Methane appears in 4 table rows, but no methane smoke point was found: the flames reached the copper plate at the end of the duct first.

Hardware discrepancies between the documents: duct size (172 x 43 x 43 mm in the final report vs ~76 x 76 mm cross-section in the papers), fuel bottle size (150 ml vs 75 cc) and MFC make (MKS vs Sierra).
Flames reached steady state within ~5 s of ignition or of a flow change; periodic flame motion was seen at high coflow, with large burners and long flames.
SPICE flow-duct hardware was later reused (slightly modified) by BASS (PSI-26).
The final report's table lists 52 smoke points while its closing remarks and the 2011 paper give 55.
526 flames were ignited against 84 planned in the SRD, because the crew became faster with the apparatus and fuel was left over.

The PSI file 'Spice Flight Test Data II modified.xls' (master sheet of ISS tests) covers only GMT days 045–062 of 2009: 154 flames in 170 data rows, with air velocity 3.5–66.5 cm/s, fuel flow 0.16–4.40 mg/s and flame length 2.3–110.6 mm. Its pressure column is a constant 101325 Pa, which confirms that pressure was assumed, not measured.
key_results: Increasing the co-flow velocity increases the smoke-point flame length; a smaller nozzle also increases it.
Smoke-point length scales with nozzle diameter to the power -0.91 times air velocity to the power 0.41.
Sooting tendency in microgravity increases from ethylene to propane, 50 % propylene, 75 % propylene and propylene. This matches normal gravity except that ethylene and propane swap places.
Luminous flame length at the smoke point is proportional to fuel mass flow rate.
Residence time helps explain the trends but does not give a quantitative correlation of the smoke points.
No smoke point could be found for methane: the flames reached the end of the duct first.

record.name: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
record.approach: Two-dimensional simulations of the formation and growth of dibutyl phthalate (DBP) smoke particles in a geometry similar to the SAME experiments. Room-temperature air (300 K) enters a long channel and flows over a heated rectangular sample (473.2 K) that releases DBP vapor at a constant mass flux of 8.4e-5 kg/(m2 s), representative of SAME mass-loss data. The compressible Navier-Stokes, energy and species equations are solved with a second-order MacCormack scheme on a 960 x 240 non-uniform grid. The particle size distribution is discretized into 45 nodes (volume ratio 2.25), with nucleation (classical theory with Girshick-Chiu correction), coagulation (Dahneke-corrected kernel), condensation/evaporation, thermophoresis (Talbot) and Stokes settling. Four base cases (8 and 10 cm/s inlet speed, Earth gravity and microgravity) plus four sensitivity cases (no settling, no thermophoresis, source rotated 90 degrees in both gravities) are compared at t = 7 s. Particle size distributions are computed from the particle flux through a plane 26 source thicknesses downstream.
record.conditions_note: Nominal values: the simulated gas is air at atmospheric pressure (outlet boundary Patm); oxygen is not modeled as a separate species, so 21 % O2 and 14.7 psi are assumed values for air at 1 atm. Inlet air and wall temperature 300 K; heated source 473.2 K; DBP mass flux 8.4e-5 kg/(m2 s); results taken at t = 7 s (effective steady state).
record.flow: Laminar, steady forced cross-flow of air entering from the left at Uo = 0.08 m/s (the SAME flow speed) or 0.10 m/s, giving Re = 22.3 or 27.7 and Fr = 0.385 or 0.481 in Earth gravity (infinite in microgravity). Recirculating wakes form behind the heated source.
record.geometry: 2D rectangular channel of height 6.82 Lo (Lo = 4.4 mm, the thickness of the heated source) with isothermal no-slip upper and lower walls; heated rectangular DBP source of thickness Lo and length 2.5 Lo placed 11 Lo downstream of the inlet; channel length about 40 Lo; particle size distributions sampled at x0 = 26 Lo downstream of the source. Sensitivity cases rotate the source 90 degrees.
record.gravity_note: Simulations at g = 0 m/s2 (microgravity) and g = 9.81 m/s2 (Earth gravity) with otherwise identical conditions
record.hardware_note: No flight hardware; numerical study based on the geometry and conditions of the SAME experiment (PSI-102) flown in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox. In-house validated compressible flow and aerosol code.
record.investigators_note: PSI roles: Principal Investigator Sean C. Garrick (University of Illinois); Technical Point of Contact Michael Hicks (NASA GRC). The final report is authored by Sean C. Garrick alone.
record.objective: Use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective: quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth-gravity smoke and identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause them.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: Numerical study of pre-fire (pyrolysis/smoldering) smoke in air at 1 atm and low forced flow; no flames, oxygen or pressure variation. Relevant to smoke detection rather than flammability.
record.space_benefits: Explains why smoke particles in spacecraft are larger than on Earth (no settling, longer residence in hot vapor-rich recirculation), supporting the design and calibration of smoke detectors for the ISS and future vehicles, since detectors calibrated for terrestrial smoke may have the wrong particle-size sensitivity.
record.study_type: numerical (2D direct numerical simulation of a compressible laminar flow with a nodal/sectional aerosol model); no flight experiment
record.earth_benefits: Models and tools that relate temperature, gravity and material properties to smoke particle characteristics can lead to better smoke detection and fire prevention.
record.fuel_state: vapor (surrogate pyrolysis vapor released from a heated solid sample)
record.hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, and the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (particle precursors) and the particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the smoke.
fuel: dibutyl phthalate (DBP) vapor, used as a surrogate for the smoldering/pyrolysis materials of the SAME experiments
data_quality_notes: This is a numerical (ground) investigation: there are no measured data; all quantities are simulation outputs.
DBP is a surrogate for the materials burned in SAME, chosen because its properties are well known.
O2 and pressure are nominal values for air at 1 atm; oxygen is not modeled separately.
The simulation is two-dimensional and laminar; particles are assumed spherical, in thermal equilibrium with the gas, with no momentum exchange, and to stick to walls with 100 % efficiency.
Results are shown at t = 7 s; the aerosol is not strictly steady in the recirculation regions.
The PSI page lists no publications; the final report says a manuscript would be submitted to Aerosol Science & Technology.
PSI lists the PI affiliation as the University of Illinois; the final report title page does not state an affiliation.

The particle size distribution summary in test_summary comes from the PSI .dat files (the full curves are in those files). The node spacing is coarse (volume ratio 2.25, diameter ratio about 1.31), so the mode diameters (5.4 or 7.1 um) are the node sizes nearest to the about 5 um stated in the report. In the data files, case 2EG also shows a small secondary peak near 21 um.
key_results: In Earth gravity buoyancy makes all fields asymmetric and carries vapor toward the cool upper wall, where nucleation is strongly enhanced (about 1e14 vs 1e12 m-3 s-1 in microgravity).
Gravitational settling removes large particles in Earth gravity: maximum size about 40 um and a single mode near 5 um at 8 cm/s.

Without buoyancy or settling, the microgravity plume is symmetric and contains very large particles (> 40 um); with a prominent hot recirculating wake behind the source the size distribution is bimodal (about 5 um and about 30 um).
Turning off settling in Earth gravity gives a bimodal distribution similar to microgravity, confirming settling as a key difference.
Thermophoresis keeps particles away from the hot source; without it particles evaporate near the source and fewer large particles form.
Rotating the source 90 degrees shrinks the wake: the large-particle mode disappears and the microgravity mode diameter is about 10 um, roughly twice the Earth-gravity value.
Increasing the flow speed from 8 to 10 cm/s reduces the effect of buoyancy and delays interaction with the upper wall.

record.name: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
record.approach: A 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity was built in OpenFOAM, coupling variable-density Navier-Stokes flow with low-temperature chemistry, heat and mass transfer, and radiation. After checking the model against ISS FLEX measurements, controlled simulations examined three forcing modes: (i) convection alone, to mimic droplet drift; (ii) imposed heat flux; (iii) convection plus heating, for large (1 to 4 mm) and sub-millimeter (about 0.5 mm) droplets. The work started with simplified chemistry and moved to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases) and pressure. Ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off ratio and extinction diameter were extracted from each case to build stability maps for cool-flame onset, persistence and quenching, which were compared with FLEX observations and used to guide future test matrices.
record.conditions_note: Simulated conditions. Ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases) and pressure were varied in parameter sweeps, but values are not given on the record.
record.flow: imposed convection to mimic droplet drift, including oscillatory or shear inflow (simulated); amplitudes and frequencies not given on the record
record.geometry: isolated spherical droplet in microgravity, simulated in 3-D; large droplets of 1 to 4 mm and sub-millimeter droplets of about 0.5 mm
record.gravity_note: simulated microgravity; model validated against ISS FLEX flight data
record.hardware_note: No hardware: computational study (PSI record lists no associated hardware).
record.investigators_note: Citation on the PSI record: Farouk T, Hicks M. Proposal title is the same as the investigation title.
record.objective: Use FLEX flight data from PSI to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations controlled the dynamics and final fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by separating the roles of deliberate heating and unintended drift-induced convection. For small and large droplets, map stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transition to hot ignition and warm-flame behaviour, and extinction in microgravity, and produce reusable models and sensitivity analyses coupling low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiation.

It informs models of cool-flame persistence and extinction rather than material selection.
record.space_benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame and extinction behaviour in microgravity; uses FLEX data to help define safer operating envelopes and materials.

record.earth_benefits: Advances understanding of low-temperature combustion relevant to engine knock, efficiency and emissions, and provides validated CFD tools transferable to practical combustors.
record.hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory or shear inflow) govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy is suppressed, this forcing was expected to dominate transport.

record.name: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
record.approach: Using the FLEX flight conditions, the effect of oxygen concentration on cool-flame extinction limits was compared with three numerical schemes: (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of an n-heptane/air mixture; (b) one-dimensional freely propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method; (c) cool-flame regimes and burning limits of DME/air at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm). Ground measurements used ozone-sensitized counterflow flames (per the objectives and the experimental table). Details are in the publications 'Dynamics of cool flames' (doi 10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787), 'Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames' (doi 10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019) and 'Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction' (doi 10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028).
record.conditions_note: Oxygen concentration was varied but values are not given on the record. The 20 atm (about 294 psi) maximum applies to the DME/air simulations; pressures of the laboratory experiments are not given.

record.investigators_note: Co-Investigator: Christopher B. Reuter (Princeton University). Frequent co-authors on the listed publications: Omar R. Yehia, Sang Hee Won, Mengni Zhou, Eric Lin and Tanvir I. Farouk.
record.objective: Using FLEX flight data from PSI, run new simulations and ground experiments with ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to: (1) build a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusion cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion and convection; (2) connect the flammability and extinction limits of hot and cool flames; (3) verify phenomena seen in the ISS FLEX experiments; (4) obtain quantitative data on extinction limits, flame temperature and species distributions to validate kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames; (5) extend cool-flame studies from ISS droplets to a more general one-dimensional ground system with radiation, diffusion, convection and low-temperature chemistry.

Informs cool-flame and extinction models rather than material selection.
record.space_benefits: Warm and cool diffusion flames matter in microgravity because of the long residence times possible there; the work helps explain how flames move between hot, warm and cool regimes near extinction, which relates to the FLEX observations on the ISS.
record.study_type: ground laboratory experiments (ozone-sensitized counterflow flames) and numerical modeling, using ISS FLEX data from PSI as reference
record.earth_benefits: Relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flows and to high-pressure near-limit combustion in engines (20 to 40 atm); the calculations advance understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and guide experiments on different flame regimes.
record.hypothesis: Oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion and convection control the transition from hot flames to cool flames; the investigation asks which conditions cause this transition and how the cool-flame flammable region relates to the hot-flame flammability and extinction limits.

record.name: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
record.approach: Spherical diffusion flames on a porous burner in microgravity, in two rounds. Normal flames (March to June 2021): fuel, pure or diluted with nitrogen, flows from the burner into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. Inverse flames (July to October 2021): an oxygen/nitrogen mixture of up to 85 % oxygen flows from the burner into a chamber filled with nitrogen and fuel, giving an inside-out flame. One extra normal-flame day was added on 18 October 2021. Ethane replaced n-pentane, whose vapor pressure was too low.
record.conditions_note: The O2 range combines two different configurations; see test_summary. In normal flames O2 is the chamber atmosphere (18 to 40 %). In inverse flames O2 is the gas leaving the burner (12 to 85 %) while the chamber holds fuel and nitrogen with no oxygen, so 85 % is not an ambient oxygen level. Pressures are approximate values from the experiment tables, converted from bar.
record.flow: no forced external flow; gas issues radially from the burner. Burner flow rate was a test variable (fuel 0.1 to 3.2 mg/s in normal flames; oxygen about 0.9 to 9.1 mg/s in inverse flames)
record.geometry: porous spherical burner, 6.35 mm diameter, in the ACME chamber insert (about 0.4 m diameter); spherical flame around the burner
record.gravity_note: ISS; about 30 s of steady microgravity is needed for these flames, which drop towers cannot provide
record.hardware_note: ACME chamber insert in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). Reused the spherical porous burners and gas delivery of ACME Flame Design and the diagnostics of the CFI droplet experiment. Retracting resistive igniter. Tests are set up by the crew and run from the ground. Known shortcoming: the burners did not always give spherically symmetric flames.
record.investigators_note: Co-Investigators: Richard L. Axelbaum (Washington University in St. Louis), Forman A. Williams (UC San Diego). Selected for flight by NSF and CASIS rather than NASA. An extension of ACME's Flame Design experiment and a follow-on to the droplet Cool Flames Investigation (CFI).
record.objective: Find the conditions under which cool diffusion flames (low-temperature flames, peak 500-1000 K) occur with gaseous fuels on a spherical burner, for normal and inverse flames and a broad range of dilution, flame temperature, flow rate and pressure. Support the tests with CFD and identify a chemical kinetics mechanism that matches the ISS measurements.
record.scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: the normal-flame tests cover ambient oxygen from 18 to 40 % at 0.5 to 3 bar, which brackets the lunar-base atmosphere (about 30 % oxygen or more at 10.2 psi, about 0.7 bar). The fuel is gas on a burner, not a solid material, so it informs models rather than material selection.
record.space_benefits: Not the focus of the investigation (the report notes that only one ACME experiment, BRE, targeted spacecraft fire safety). Useful to fire safety as data on flames at high oxygen concentration and at pressures from about half to three atmospheres, and on cool flames that persist or reignite after a hot flame goes out.
record.study_type: experimental (flight experiment on the ISS), supported by CFD simulations
record.earth_benefits: Tests and advances cool-flame chemical kinetics mechanisms, which should help develop cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines (ultra-lean combustion could raise engine thermal efficiency from about 38 % toward 60 %).
record.funding: National Science Foundation (NSF) / Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS)
record.hypothesis: ISS testing can demonstrate for the first time: steady cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners; cool diffusion flames of propane, n-butane and n-pentane; cool flames over a wide range of conditions and pressures; inverse cool diffusion flames; and cool flames that extinguish when flow decreases and switch to a hot flame when flow increases, with possible oscillation between hot and cool flames.
record.principal_investigator: Peter B. Sunderland (University of Maryland, Fire Protection Engineering)
data_quality_notes: The 'Cool flame?' column of the normal-flame table is filled in for only 8 tests; an empty cell does not mean no cool flame was looked for.
A few cells contain spreadsheet errors (#DIV/0!, #VALUE!) and one day of inverse tests (day 8) lost most of its data.
The inverse-flame table has several hundred empty rows after the data, and 'inverse' is written with and without a capital letter.
The final report is dated November 2022 and states that data analysis was still under way.
key_results: Spherical cool diffusion flames burning gases were observed for the first time.
Cool flames were hard to produce: they were obtained only for normal n-butane flames at about 2 bar with about 39 % ambient oxygen. The hot flames they followed were 2.6 times as large.
A cool flame can reignite into a hot flame: on the added test day, platinum in an exposed thermocouple near the burner catalyzed hot-flame reignition from the cool flames.
One test recorded five transitions from hot flame to cool flame (six hot and five cool flames in sequence).
Burner temperature has an important effect on these cool flames; they sit in fuel-rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.
Highest oxygen levels of any microgravity test in PSI: 79 inverse-flame tests with 85 % oxygen flowing from the burner, at pressures from about 0.55 to 3.3 bar.

From the experiment table: normal flames in about 21 % ambient oxygen self-extinguished within about 20 s, while at 35 to 40 % oxygen flames burned for up to five minutes or until the flow was stopped.

From the experiment table: with 85 % oxygen from the burner, inverse flames at about 0.55 bar burned until the flow was stopped, while at 2.2 and 3.3 bar almost all self-extinguished. The chamber fuel fraction also differed between these test days, so pressure is not the only factor.
On the ground, cool diffusion flames were also observed for the first time near the surface of a liquid fuel pool (n-heptane), with peak temperatures of 705 to 760 K.
